display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

contextLabel.description: Short header tying the suggestion to the user request.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

keywords.description: Topic keywords from the user's request.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value. Rename a doc only when asked to, not to change a link's text. It may be one the given doc links to: read its tabs' text to see links.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

Read the result before you start the task anew or do it here: after "Not withdrawn", do neither.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - The user is applying for an FDE role at Moveo group. The home assignment (ASSIGNMENT.pdf) is to build a "Weather Risk Intelligence Agent" for a US logistics company that ranks distribution hubs by weather-disruption exposure. It must:
     - answer the sample questions (Midwest winter exposure; Miami vs Houston hurricane and flood; % of Denver days with snowfall last year; why Dallas is high);
     - use public APIs, include deterministic scoring, a chat UI (voice is a bonus), an API used by the UI, JSON-schema enforcement between the LLM and code, an eval set with a runner, and clear assumptions and uncertainty;
     - bonus: a scheduled or webhook alert when a hub's risk score changes.
   - Deliverables: source code with run instructions (live demo; a deployed URL is preferred), a short design/architecture doc (architecture, repo structure, data storage choice), and **the full AI session transcript (mandatory)**.
   - The user wants to **submit tonight; nothing can change after submission.** Tomorrow: a review and Q&A for the interview.
   - The current agreed plan:
     1. **Phase 12 docs** (DESIGN.md, DECISIONS.md, README polish);
     2. **Voice** (mic button + read-aloud via browser Web Speech API, ~45 min);
     3. **Phase 11 deploy to Render** (Dockerfile; the user clicks in Render and sets environment variables);
     4. optional Phase 9 as **live NWS active-warning alerts**, only if at least 1.5 h remains;
     5. **Phase 13**: fresh-clone test, tests, short eval run, **export the transcript last**, final push.
   - MCP (Phase 10) is skipped and goes in the design doc as future work.
   - User instruction for the docs (verbatim): "make sure when you write the documentation to not use ai symbols and write clear explanations and if needed, the thought process and decision making".
   - Earlier standing preferences:
     - client-friendly UI (technical details hidden behind a developer view);
     - no AI-looking text (no em/en dashes or ellipses) in the UI or in agent answers;
     - determinism: parameters need a rationale or a data test chosen before seeing rankings; no tuning to expected results;
     - answers must keep full information (latency matters less than completeness).

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Python 3.12.7 (Anaconda) venv; FastAPI/uvicorn; SQLite (WITHOUT ROWID tables after compaction); pandas 3.1.1, numpy, scipy (Poisson and Clopper-Pearson intervals); httpx; pydantic v2 strict models; openai 3.57.0 Responses API (function tools with strict:true, `text.format` json_schema, `reasoning.effort`, usage with cached_tokens).
   - The model is gpt-6.2-sol ($2 input / $0.10 cached / $10 output per 1M tokens); cost is tracked per call.
   - **Agent loop:** LLM picks tools → `registry.execute` → FinalAnswer JSON → validator. The validator traces every number in the answer text to a tool-result field (exact/rounded preferred over share-as-percent; most recent output wins). One retry, then visible warnings. Text is then cleaned deterministically (`textclean`). Sessions are our own in-memory history, with old tool outputs trimmed.
   - **KPIs:**
     - routine (warning) days per year = NWS warning days (IEM VTEC archive 2006–2025; zone/county products by UGC; storm polygons only if they contain the hub);
     - **disaster-level days** = warning days × FEMA major-disaster severity share, pooled across hubs. A declaration matches a hazard by incident type OR by title regex. This is the primary ranking;
     - no subjective weights; optional analyst `day_costs`; tiers are thirds; confidence comes from rules; 90% ranges are conservative.
   - Evidence data: GHCN-Daily airport stations 1996–2025 (station-first, Open-Meteo fills gaps), HURDAT2 1950–2025 (150 km), SPC 1996–2025 (50 km, report days), FEMA NRI AFREQ (stand-in similarity only), Census gazetteer places + population 2025.
   - **Seasonal outlook** (`hub_monthly`): per month, % of years with at least one warning day, plus a binomial range. **Season profiles** (`hub_hazard_season`): usual months, typical dates, events per year, typical and longest event.
   - **Stand-in** `find_nearest_hubs`:
     - matching steps: hub name → namesake check (another place ≥ 50,000 people with the same name means ambiguous) → exact/alias/prefix/fuzzy matching → population rule for ambiguity;
     - 3 nearest hubs; score = 0.8 × FEMA-profile similarity + 0.2 × proximity (zero at 500 km); tie margin 2 points → the closer hub wins;
     - coverage = the network's widest hub gap (622 km, Billings); outside it → `outside_coverage`;
     - the LLM converts nicknames to official names and says so.
   - **API protection:** X-Access-Code, 10 chats/min per IP, daily budget $3 (raise at runtime via POST /api/admin/budget with X-Admin-Token), LLMUnavailableError → 502.
   - **UI:** plain HTML/JS, marked + DOMPurify + Inter font stored in the repo, design tokens for light/dark, outlook cards, leaderboard, hub drawer, methodology modal, developer view (`?dev=1` or the methodology toggle).

3. Files and Code Sections (repo weather-risk-agent/, all committed through 96ccc41):
   - **app/config.py:** settings for:
     - openai_api_key, llm_model="gpt-6.2-sol", llm_reasoning_effort="medium", llm_max_output_tokens=6000, agent_max_steps=8;
     - prices; app_access_code="", admin_token="", chat_rate_limit_per_min=10, daily_budget_usd=3.0, cors_origins, db_path.
   - **app/db.py:** schema for hubs, daily_weather (no weather_code), nri_county(county_fips, hazard, afreq, nri_version), places (incl. aland_sqmi, population), storm_tracks, severe_reports, hub_event_rates, hub_stations (gust_measured), station_daily, hub_ugc, nws_warnings, fema_declarations (title), hub_monthly, hub_hazard_season, hub_metrics, risk_scores, alerts, ingest_log. `get_connection` uses timeout=120.
   - **app/ingest/**: hubs.py (FIPS via FCC; upsert), fema_nri.py (ArcGIS paging; AFREQ only), census_gazetteer.py (`clean_place_name` strips the suffix once; nearest county centroid; `load_population`), open_meteo.py, hurdat2.py, spc_reports.py (browser UA), ghcn.py (WSF5 required + fallback; pre-filter on fallback elements), nws_warnings.py (points API, IEM byugc + sbw_by_point, OpenFEMA declarations filtered to hub counties), build_db.py (steps: hubs, nri, census, weather, hurdat2, spc, ghcn, warnings, rates, score [+ seasonal]), compact_db.py (latest run only, WITHOUT ROWID, empties raw tables, VACUUM), common.py.
   - **app/scoring/params.yaml** (params_version "1.2"): event_rates radii/files; stations rules; scoring (kpi_version "3.0", thresholds, descriptive thresholds, default_day_costs, confidence_rules); warnings (phenomena map, polygon_url, polygon_phenomena [SV, TO, FF, FA, EW, DS]); declarations (DR, incident_types, `title_patterns`, e.g. winter `'\bWINTER\b|BLIZZARD|\bSNOW(?!\s?MELT)|ICE STORM|\bICE\b(?!\s+JAMS?)|FREEZ'`); stand_in (candidates 3, w_similarity 0.8, w_proximity 0.2, proximity_zero_km 500, far_caveat_km 250, tie_margin 2.0, coverage: network_widest_gap, major_place_population 50000, population_file, fuzzy_cutoff 0.85).
   - **app/scoring/**: metrics.py (combine_variable, rate_with_interval, disruption_flags, warning_days with format="ISO8601", dates_in_incidents, share_with_interval), engine.py (hub_evidence, `declarations_for_hazard`, severity_shares, score_all, latest_breakdown), event_rates.py (epoch fix, hurricane_days with dates), seasonal.py (monthly_rows, `season_profile`, compute), params.py.
   - **app/tools/**: schemas.py (HubId enum from hubs.yaml; inputs incl. SeasonalOutlookInput; day_costs only with hazard='all'), hub_tools.py (list_hubs, rank_hubs [shared ranks, no_exposure_in_data, range_90pct, about_once_every_years, tier vs overall_tier], compare_hubs ["tie"/"none" verdicts, season], get_hub_risk_breakdown [contributions, season per hazard, monthly pattern, FEMA disasters, station, confidence], get_weather_stat, get_methodology, get_seasonal_outlook; SOURCES/EVIDENCE_SOURCES in plain language; `every_years`), locate.py (find_nearest_hubs, `network_widest_gap_km`), registry.py (TOOLS, strict_schema, openai_tools, execute).
   - **app/agent/**: llm_client.py (only OpenAI module; LLMUnavailableError; cost), answer_schema.py (FinalAnswer without figures/data_sources; code adds them), prompts.py (rules: copy numbers from tools, disaster-level wording with once-every-N-years, pair with warning days, season fields, stand-in flow with nickname conversion and "say so", always call the tool even if ambiguous, outside_coverage, false premise, heat, out of scope, seasonal outlook as not a forecast, no dashes or filler), validator.py (trace_figures, data_sources, rank and stand-in checks), textclean.py (clean_text/clean_answer), sessions.py, agent.py, cli.py.
   - **app/api/**: main.py (endpoints /api/chat, /api/chat/reset, /api/scores, /api/hubs, /api/hubs/{id}/breakdown, /api/outlook, /api/methodology, /api/admin/budget, /health, static `/`), guards.py.
   - **web/**: index.html, styles.css, app.js (client view with "Sources & reliability", developer view, outlook, leaderboard "Disaster-level"/"Warning days", drawer with season lines and EVIDENCE_LABELS, `oncePer`, `fill`, New chat hidden until there's a thread, months 1–12), vendor/marked.min.js 12.0.2, vendor/purify.min.js 3.1.6, fonts/inter-latin-wght-normal.woff2.
   - **evals/**: cases.yaml (20 cases), checks.py (get_path, oracle, value_in_text, args_match, check_turn), run_evals.py (`--case`, `--category`, `--repeat`, `--model`, `--threshold`; writes eval-latest.json). results/eval-latest.json, smoke.json and smoke_v2.json are committed; smoke.py was removed.
   - **tests/**: test_scoring, test_locate, test_tools, test_agent, test_api, test_seasonal, test_event_rates, test_textclean, test_eval_checks (125 passing).
   - **README.md:** quickstart, API table, CLI, tests, evals section, rebuild. **PLAN.md** still contains em dashes in its headings ("Phase 2 — ..."), to be cleaned.
   - Memory file: `C:\Users\97254\.claude\projects\C--Users-97254-Downloads-Moveo-Assignment\memory\moveo-assignment-context.md` (+ MEMORY.md).

4. Errors and fixes (main ones):
   - `python` is the Store alias → the venv was built from the Anaconda path. PowerShell mangles inline Python, so scripts run from files in the scratchpad.
   - Open-Meteo hourly limit → caching and a resumable delayed rerun. hazards.fema.gov refused connections → used the ArcGIS service.
   - NRI risk score is exposure-driven → switched to AFREQ. Percentile flattening and county-area bias for tornadoes → radius counts.
   - GHCN prefix slicing bug; the WSF5 inventory pre-filter excluded stations; the deleted/emptied station table race.
   - pandas 3 datetime resolution collapsed hurricane dates to 1970 → epoch via Timedelta, plus a regression test.
   - Mixed ISO formats → `format="ISO8601"`. County-polygon bias for flood warnings → point query (sbw_by_point).
   - Repeated suffix stripping ("Kansas City" → "Kansas") → strip once. The Portland namesake check.
   - Validator regex missed "within_150km" → lookbehind `[A-Za-z0-9.]`. Exact-vs-percent misattribution → exact matches first.
   - FEMA titles missing from the cached file → re-downloaded through the ingest code. replaceChildren rendered null as text → `fill` helper.
   - The DB was 97 MB → compact_db brought it to about 49 MB.
   - User feedback incorporated:
     - equal weights rejected → disaster-days approach → NWS + FEMA severity;
     - shorten answers? No, keep the information;
     - client-friendly UI;
     - New chat confusion;
     - month numbers;
     - flood/winter discussion (kept classification by mechanism);
     - make fixes general, not specific;
     - nicknames/ZIP codes are overkill → prompt rule + network coverage only.

5. Problem Solving:
   - Phase 8 is complete: 40/40 runs pass. The Springfield fix forces the tool call.
   - The stand-in sweep over 48 places was reviewed.
   - Ongoing: writing the documentation.

6. All user messages (paraphrased; security-relevant content kept):

   - Copied .env and added the key. Commit + push → gave the repo URL https://github.com/omrikantor/weather-risk-agent.
   - Phase 2 questions about the hub list, unknown hubs and the tables; stand-in ideas (nearest hub, then climate matching); data problems 13/16/17; radii and determinism concerns ("make sure we are not changing the data according to your previous knowledge"); approved A and B.
   - Asked to continue while downloads ran; commit; asked about weights (didn't like equal weights); asked whether FEMA building loss is right → NWS warnings; "is that the best way"; go with NWS warnings quickly.
   - Asked what data is used; cleanup; review of each tool; fixes 1, 4, 5, 6 (accepted 2 and 3).
   - Phase 5 approvals; why cost tracking; faster answers (keep full info); answer sizes.
   - Phase 6: cap too low → $3 adjustable. Phase 7: no voice for now; keep the leaderboard; "very aesthetic and professional"; seasonal outlook idea.
   - New chat didn't work; client-friendly, not developer-facing. Month numbers; is 0.36 days realistic.
   - Wanted timing information; "yes" to the FEMA title fix, wording and seasons.
   - Flood vs winter question; remove AI-looking text ("like longer '-'"); test non-hub places.
   - Tie rule yes; wanted general fixes; what to do with AK/HI/PR; nicknames/ZIP overkill; determinism question about the prompt rule; continue the fix.
   - Phase 8 steps; start; asked if Phase 8 finished.

# Weather Risk Intelligence Agent: Design This document explains how the system is built and why. The decision history, including the options we rejected, is in [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md). ## 1. What the system does A logistics company runs distribution hubs across the US and wants to know which hubs are most exposed to weather disruption, so it can decide where to invest in resilience upgrades. The system gives its analysts: - A **chat agent** that answers questions such as "Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter disruption?", "Compare Miami and Houston for hurricanes and flooding", "What percentage of days in Denver last year had snowfall?" and "Why is the Dallas hub high?". It handles follow-up questions in the same conversation. - A **ranking (leaderboard)** of all 47 hubs, filterable by hazard and region, and a **hub detail panel** with the evidence behind each score. - A **seasonal outlook** for the current month: which hubs historically face the most disruption in that month, from which hazard, and how often it happened. The central design rule: **the language model never produces numbers.** All scores and statistics are computed by deterministic Python code from public data. The model decides which tools to call and explains the results in plain language. Code then checks that every number in the answer appears in a tool result before the answer is shown. ## 2. Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Offline build SRC[Public data sources
NWS, FEMA, NOAA, Census, Open-Meteo] --> ING[Ingestion
app/ingest] ING --> DB[(SQLite
data/risk.db)] DB --> SCORE[Scoring engine
app/scoring] SCORE --> DB end subgraph Running service UI[Web UI
web/] -->|HTTP JSON| API[FastAPI
app/api] API -->|chat| AGENT[Agent loop
app/agent] AGENT <-->|Responses API| LLM[OpenAI gpt-6.2-sol] AGENT --> TOOLS[Tools
app/tools] API -->|leaderboard, outlook, hub details| TOOLS TOOLS --> DB AGENT --> VAL[Validator
number tracing] end ``` **Two halves.** The left half runs once (or whenever the data is refreshed): it downloads public data, stores it in SQLite and computes the scores. The right half is the running web service, which only reads the database. This split keeps answers fast and reproducible, and the live demo does not depend on any external data API being available. **Components and how they talk to each other** | Component | Responsibility | Talks to | |---|---|---| | Web UI (`web/`) | Chat, seasonal outlook, leaderboard, hub details, methodology. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step | FastAPI over HTTP/JSON | | FastAPI (`app/api/main.py`) | Chat endpoint, data endpoints, health check, access code, rate limit, daily spend cap | Agent, tools | | Agent (`app/agent/agent.py`) | Runs the conversation: sends the question to the model, executes the tools it asks for, validates the final answer | OpenAI (through `llm_client.py` only), tools, validator | | Tools (`app/tools/`) | Eight deterministic functions: rank, compare, explain a hub, weather statistics, seasonal outlook, methodology, list hubs, find a stand-in hub | SQLite | | Validator (`app/agent/validator.py`) | Traces every number in the answer to a tool-result field; checks ranks and stand-in behavior | Tool outputs of the session | | Scoring engine (`app/scoring/`) | Computes the risk measures, uncertainty ranges, monthly and seasonal statistics | SQLite | | Ingestion (`app/ingest/`) | Downloads and caches the public data, builds the database | Public APIs and files | **The life of one chat request** 1. The UI sends `POST /api/chat` with the message and the session id. 2. The API checks the access code, the per-IP rate limit and the daily budget. 3. The agent adds today's date and the message to the session history and calls the model with the system prompt, the tool definitions and the required answer format. 4. The model asks for one or more tools, for example `rank_hubs(hazard="winter", region="Midwest")`. The agent validates the arguments against the tool's schema, runs the tool and returns the result to the model. This repeats (at most 8 steps) until the model writes its final answer. 5. The final answer is JSON in a fixed format. The validator parses it, traces every number in the text to a tool result, checks ranks against the tools and checks that a recommended stand-in hub is not analyzed without the user's confirmation. If something fails, the model gets one retry with the specific problems listed. 6. Code attaches the traced figures and the data sources, removes typographic artifacts (dashes, ellipses) and returns the answer with a trace of the tool calls, the token usage, the cost and the latency. ## 3. Repository structure ``` weather-risk-agent/ README.md how to run, test and evaluate DESIGN.md this document DECISIONS.md decision log with alternatives and reasons PLAN.md the implementation plan written at the start (kept as part of the AI session record) requirements.txt pinned Python dependencies .env.example configuration template (API key, access code, limits) app/ config.py settings from .env (model, effort, prices for cost tracking, limits) db.py SQLite schema geo.py distance helpers ingest/ one module per data source, plus build_db.py (build) and compact_db.py (shrink for git) scoring/ params.yaml every method parameter, versioned, with the reason for each engine.py risk measures, severity shares, tiers, confidence, hub breakdown metrics.py daily data (station first, model data as backup) and day-based statistics event_rates.py hurricane and severe-storm rates around each hub seasonal.py monthly outlook and per-hazard season profiles tools/ schemas.py input models for every tool (become strict JSON schemas) registry.py tool list, schema conversion, validated execution hub_tools.py the tool functions locate.py find_nearest_hubs (place lookup and stand-in recommendation) agent/ llm_client.py the only module that talks to OpenAI answer_schema.py the final answer format the model must return prompts.py system prompt validator.py number tracing and behavior checks textclean.py removes dashes and ellipses from answers sessions.py conversation memory agent.py the agent loop cli.py command-line chat api/ main.py FastAPI app guards.py access code, rate limit, daily budget web/ index.html, styles.css, app.js, plus vendored libraries and font data/ hubs.yaml the hub list (configuration, not code) risk.db the built database (committed so the app runs without downloading anything) evals/ cases.yaml, checks.py, run_evals.py, results/ tests/ unit and integration tests (no OpenAI calls) docs/ai-session/ the exported AI session ``` ## 4. Data ### 4.1 Sources and what each one is used for | Source | Period | What we take | Used for | |---|---|---|---| | NWS warnings (Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive of National Weather Service warnings) | 2006 to 2025 | Every warning issued for each hub's forecast zone and county; storm-based warnings only when the warning polygon contains the hub | **Main measure**: days per year with a warning, per hazard | | FEMA disaster declarations (OpenFEMA) | 1996 to 2025 | Major disasters in each hub's county, with type, title and incident dates | **Severity**: how often a warning day turned into a federally declared disaster | | NOAA GHCN-Daily (airport weather stations) | 1996 to 2025 | Daily rain, snow, temperature, peak gusts and observed events (thunder, hail, freezing rain, ice pellets) | Evidence (snow days, heavy rain days, ice days) and weather statistics questions | | Open-Meteo (historical reanalysis) | 2016 to 2026 | Daily weather on a grid | Fills gaps in station data; the current year | | NOAA HURDAT2 (hurricane tracks) | 1950 to 2025 | Every Atlantic and Northeast Pacific storm track | Evidence: storms per decade within 150 km, named storms, 10-year probability | | NOAA SPC (severe storm reports) | 1996 to 2025 | Tornado, hail and wind reports with coordinates | Evidence: report days within 50 km | | FEMA National Risk Index | December 2025 version | Annual event frequency per hazard for every US county | Comparing a non-hub place with nearby hubs (stand-in recommendation) | | Census Gazetteer and population estimates | 2026 and 2025 | Every US place with coordinates, land area and population | Finding non-hub places and resolving ambiguous names | | NWS points API, FCC Area API | current | Each hub's forecast zone, county and time zone | Linking hubs to warnings and FEMA records | All raw downloads are cached in `data/raw/` (not in git). `python -m app.ingest.build_db` rebuilds the whole database from that cache; a full rebuild reproduced every hub score exactly. ### 4.2 Why SQLite The data is small and read-only while the service runs: about 515,000 station-days, 187,000 model-days, 32,000 places and 13,000 warnings, 49 MB in total. SQLite needs no server, ships inside the container as a single file, gives the tools plain SQL and makes the build reproducible: the file in git is exactly what the app reads. A server database (Postgres) would become the right choice when several processes write at the same time, for example a multi-user deployment that stores conversation history and alerts, or when the hub network grows to thousands of sites. The tool layer is the only code that reads the database, so the change would be contained. To keep the file under GitHub's limits, `compact_db.py` keeps only the latest scoring run, stores the large tables in SQLite's compact `WITHOUT ROWID` layout and empties the raw event tables that are only needed to recompute rates (the computed rates are kept). ### 4.3 Main tables | Table | Content | |---|---| | `hubs` | 47 hubs: id, name, state, Census region, coordinates, county | | `nws_warnings`, `hub_ugc` | Warnings per hub zone, county and point; each hub's NWS zone and time zone | | `fema_declarations` | Major disasters in hub counties | | `station_daily`, `hub_stations`, `daily_weather` | Daily weather (station and model) and the station chosen for each hub | | `hub_event_rates` | Hurricane and severe-storm rates per hub, hazard and radius, with ranges | | `risk_scores` | The scoring output: totals, per-hazard values, tier, and a full JSON breakdown per hub | | `hub_monthly`, `hub_hazard_season` | Monthly outlook statistics and per-hazard season profiles | | `places`, `nri_county` | Place lookup and county hazard profiles for stand-in recommendations | | `ingest_log` | What was downloaded and when | ## 5. How risk is measured ### 5.1 The two measures **Warning days per year** (routine disruption): for each hub and hazard, the number of days per year with a National Weather Service warning for that hazard at the hub. NWS warning criteria are set locally, so a warning means conditions expected to be dangerous for that specific place. This answers "how often does this hazard disrupt operations here?". **Disaster-level days per year** (the primary ranking): warning days multiplied by the hazard's **severity share**, which is the share of warning days that fell inside a FEMA major-disaster incident period of a matching type in the hub's county. It answers "how often does this hazard reach a level that requires federal disaster assistance?". Resilience investment protects against severe events, so this is the default ranking. Values below one day per year are also shown as "about once every N years" (for example, a disaster-level winter day in Fargo about once every 2.1 years). Current severity shares, pooled over the 47 hubs: | Hazard | Severity share | Basis | |---|---|---| | Hurricane / tropical | 46.3% | 100 of 216 warning days | | Flood | 16.7% | 559 of 3,355 | | Winter | 4.8% | 110 of 2,271 | | Thunderstorm / wind | 4.4% | 267 of 6,111 | | Heat | 0% | 0 of 2,053 | Heat is 0% because FEMA did not declare a single heat disaster in 1996 to 2025. The system explains this as "no evidence of disaster-level heat", not "heat is harmless", and still reports heat warning days. ### 5.2 How we arrived at this measure The measure went through several versions, each one corrected by evidence from the data: 1. **Fixed weather thresholds with hand-picked hazard weights** (for example snow over 5 cm, heat over 38 C, winter weight 0.25). Rejected: the weights were our judgment, not data. 2. **Disruption days from fixed thresholds, summed without weights.** Rejected after seeing the results: Phoenix and Las Vegas ranked first because 38 C days are ordinary there (106 per year in Phoenix), and a hurricane day counted the same as a hot day. 3. **FEMA building loss as a severity weight.** Rejected: property loss is not operational disruption. 4. **NWS warnings for frequency, FEMA declarations for severity** (the current method). Warnings are locally calibrated, which solves the Phoenix problem. Declarations measure what actually became a disaster, which gives hurricanes their real weight without anyone choosing it. Two data problems found along the way were fixed in general ways: - **Large counties.** Counting every flash flood or thunderstorm warning that touched Maricopa County gave Phoenix 758 flash-flood warnings; counting only warning polygons that contain the hub gives 31. Storm-based warnings are now counted only when the polygon contains the hub. - **Misfiled disasters.** FEMA often files winter disasters as "Severe Storm" or "Flood" (for example "SEVERE WINTER STORMS AND BLIZZARD CONDITIONS"). Declarations now match a hazard by type or by title keywords; snowmelt and ice-jam titles are excluded from winter because they are floods. ### 5.3 Supporting calculations - **Tiers**: High, Elevated and Low are the top, middle and bottom third of the 47 hubs by disaster-level days. The scores are relative to the network, so fixed cut-offs would not mean anything. - **Uncertainty ranges**: warning-day rates get an exact Poisson 90% interval; severity shares get an exact binomial interval; disaster-level days combine the two conservatively (the range is wider than a joint interval would be). - **Confidence per hub**: lowered when the weather station is more than 25 km away, when the station does not measure gusts and observed events, or when modeled data had to replace station data. - **Analyst weights**: an analyst can say "count hurricane days three times as costly"; the ranking then multiplies each hazard's days by that cost. Without it, every disaster-level day counts the same. In a real engagement these costs would come from the client's own closure data. - **Seasonal outlook**: for each hub, hazard and calendar month, the share of years (out of 20) with at least one warning day, with a binomial range, and the expected disaster-level days for that month. - **Season profile**: for each hub and hazard, the shortest run of months holding at least 80% of warning days, the typical date range, events per year and their typical and longest length (for example, Fargo winter: usually December 12 to March 14, about 5.3 events a year, typically 2 days). ### 5.4 Method parameters Every threshold, radius, window and pattern lives in `app/scoring/params.yaml` with the reason for its value. Parameters were chosen for a stated reason or from a data-based test before looking at rankings, and never adjusted for a single hub. Two examples of data-based tests: the hurricane and storm radii (150 km and 50 km) were chosen after checking that hub rankings stay stable across nearby radii (rank correlation 0.83 to 0.98), and the coverage limit for stand-in hubs is computed from the hub network itself (section 6). The same data and the same parameters always produce the same output. ## 6. Places that are not hubs When a user asks about a place that is not a hub (for example "a hub in Tampa"), the agent says there is no data for that place and calls `find_nearest_hubs`: 1. **Find the place** in the Census list (exact name, then known name patterns, then name prefix, then close spelling). The model converts nicknames and boroughs to official names first ("Brooklyn" to "New York, NY") and says so in the answer. 2. **Ambiguous names**: if exactly one match has at least 50,000 people (the Census threshold for the core city of a metropolitan area), use it; otherwise ask the user which one (Springfield returns Missouri, Massachusetts, Illinois, Oregon and Ohio). 3. **Coverage**: if the nearest hub is farther than the network's widest gap between neighboring hubs (622 km today), no hub is a meaningful stand-in and the agent says so. With today's network this covers every mainland place and excludes Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico, without naming any state in the rule. 4. **Recommend a stand-in** among the 3 nearest hubs: 80% hazard-profile similarity (FEMA county frequencies for 10 hazards) plus 20% proximity. Candidates within 2 points of the best are treated as tied and the closest one wins, because county-level profiles are coarse and distance is exact. 5. **Ask before analyzing** the stand-in, then label the analysis clearly as a stand-in. Examples: Tampa to Orlando, Charleston SC to Jacksonville (coastal, rather than the closer Charlotte), Spokane to Boise (inland, rather than the closer Seattle). ## 7. The contract between the language model and the code - **Tools**: each tool has a Pydantic input model converted to a strict JSON schema (every field required or explicitly nullable, no extra fields). Hub ids and regions are fixed lists, so the model cannot ask for a hub that does not exist. Invalid arguments come back to the model as an error it can correct. - **Final answer**: the model must return JSON with the answer text, question type, measure used, hubs mentioned, assumptions, uncertainty, whether it is waiting for the user's confirmation and suggested follow-ups (`app/agent/answer_schema.py`). - **Number tracing**: code finds every number in the answer text and matches it to a tool-result field (allowing display rounding and a share shown as a percentage). Untraceable numbers trigger one retry, then a visible warning. The traced list ("1.32 comes from get_hub_risk_breakdown.severe_days_per_year") is shown in the developer view. - **Why code builds the figure list**: the first version asked the model to list every number and its source. That made answers slow (about 60% of the output was this list) and relied on the model to describe its own sources. Moving the tracing into code cut output tokens by 45% and made it more reliable. - **Provider isolation**: only `llm_client.py` imports the OpenAI SDK. The rest of the code uses neutral types, so changing provider means rewriting one file. - **Cost control**: the system prompt and tool list never change, so the provider caches them (about 60% of input tokens are cached); old tool outputs are trimmed from the history; at most 8 steps per question; a daily spend cap in the API. ## 8. API and user interface | Method | Path | Purpose | |---|---|---| | POST | `/api/chat` | Ask the agent; returns the answer, traced figures, sources, tool trace, cost and latency | | POST | `/api/chat/reset` | Clear a conversation | | GET | `/api/scores` | Leaderboard (no language model) | | GET | `/api/outlook` | Seasonal outlook for a month (no language model) | | GET | `/api/hubs`, `/api/hubs/{id}/breakdown` | Hub list and hub details (no language model) | | GET | `/api/methodology` | Definitions, severity shares, sources and limitations | | POST | `/api/admin/budget` | Raise or lower the daily spend cap while running (admin token) | | GET | `/health` | Database status, data freshness, model, remaining budget | The leaderboard, outlook and hub panel use the same tool functions as the agent, so the numbers on screen and in answers always agree. **Protection for a public URL**: an access code on every `/api/*` call, 10 chat messages per minute per IP address, and a daily OpenAI spend cap (3 USD by default, adjustable at runtime) after which chat answers with a clear message while the data views keep working. **Client view and developer view**: by default the interface shows what a client needs (the answer, a confidence badge, "Sources and reliability" with a confirmation that all figures were checked against the data, plain-language evidence in the hub panel). Tool calls, field-level number tracing, tokens and cost are available in a developer view (Methodology, "Show technical details", or `?dev=1`) for demonstrations. ## 9. Testing and evaluation **Unit and integration tests** (`tests/`, 125 tests, no OpenAI calls): scoring functions on synthetic data, the tools and the place lookup on the real database, the validator and text cleanup, the agent loop with a scripted fake model, and the API including access control, rate limit, budget and outage handling. **Evaluation of the real model** (`evals/`, `python -m evals.run_evals`): 20 cases, some with several turns, covering rankings (including analyst weights), comparisons, statistics, explanations, timing and the seasonal outlook, methodology, stand-in hubs, nicknames, ambiguous and out-of-coverage places, a false premise, a follow-up and guardrails (an out-of-scope forecast question and a request to make up a number). Checks are deterministic: expected tool calls and arguments, expected figures and ranking order computed by calling the same tools directly (never hard-coded), required and forbidden phrases, question type and confirmation behavior, plus validation, completion and plain-text checks on every answer. Latest run, every case twice: **40 of 40 passed**, average 10.3 seconds and 0.013 USD per answer. The evaluations also found real problems that were then fixed (for example the model deciding on its own that "Springfield" is ambiguous instead of using the data). ## 10. Assumptions, uncertainty and limitations - **The hub network is an assumption.** The assignment does not list hubs, so we chose 47 US cities that cover every Census region and every hazard type, using city-center coordinates. For a real client, `data/hubs.yaml` would hold their actual sites; adding a hub is one line plus a rebuild. - **Regions** are US Census Bureau regions. - **Warnings are forecasts.** NWS warnings include some false alarms and misses, and their criteria and names changed over time (for example "Excessive Heat" became "Extreme Heat" in 2024; both are counted). - **Declarations are partly policy-driven.** Federal declaration thresholds depend on statewide damage per resident, and heat is essentially never declared. Incident periods are administrative and can be longer than the weather itself. - **Severity shares are pooled** across our 47 hubs, because we do not have warning data for every US county. - **Disaster-level days are not closures.** They measure how often a hazard reached disaster level near the hub, not whether this company's hub actually closed. The client's own closure and cost records would be the best calibration. - **Every disaster-level day counts the same** unless an analyst supplies day costs. - **Station data** comes from the nearest major airport (up to 31 km away); missing days are filled with modeled data, which smooths extremes. Observed-event flags are recorded inconsistently. - **Hazards are grouped by type, not by season.** A snowmelt flood counts as flooding, because the investment response (drainage, barriers) is a flood response; the season profile shows when each hazard happens. - **The past does not fully predict the future.** All figures are historical frequencies; the interface and the answers say "not a forecast". - **Language model behavior** is checked by evaluations and the validator, but a model can still word something imprecisely; numbers cannot be invented without a visible warning. ## 11. What we chose not to build, and how it would work - **Score-change alerts** (an assignment bonus): a scheduled job that refreshes recent warnings, re-scores, compares with the previous run and posts changes to a webhook. Our measures describe 20 years of history and barely change day to day, so a more useful version would alert on live NWS warnings for each hub. Not built to protect the submission timeline. - **MCP server**: exposing the same tools to any MCP-compatible assistant (for example Claude Desktop). The tool registry already has everything needed; it would be a thin wrapper. - **Assessment of any US address on demand**: the same warning-day method applied to a location's own NWS zone, using live API calls instead of the pre-built database. - **Broader place lookup**: Census county subdivisions, counties and ZIP codes. - **Client calibration**: replacing pooled severity shares and equal day costs with the client's own closure history and cost per day. - **Production concerns**: Postgres for shared state, authentication instead of an access code, monitoring of model quality and cost over time.

# Decision Log

This file records the main decisions made while building the system: what the options were, what we chose and why. Several decisions were reversed after looking at real data; those reversals are kept here because they explain why the current method looks the way it does. The design itself is described in [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md).

## D1. Overall approach: deterministic tools plus a language model that explains

**Options considered**

- A. A single agent with a fixed set of deterministic tools, plain SDK, one model.
- B. A retrieval approach where the model reads raw data or documents and reasons over them.
- C. A multi-agent or graph framework (for example LangGraph) with separate planner, analyst and writer agents.

**Choice: A.**

**Why.** The assignment asks for deterministic scoring and JSON-schema enforcement between the model and the code. With approach A every number comes from code, which can be tested, and the model's job is limited to choosing tools and explaining results, which is what it is good at. Approach B lets the model compute numbers, which cannot be verified. Approach C adds structure we did not need: the questions are answered in one to four tool calls, and a framework would add dependencies and hide the loop that we want to show and control. The agent loop is about 150 lines and easy to read.

## D2. Model provider and model

**Options considered:** Anthropic Claude models and OpenAI models; one model for everything or a small model for routing plus a large model for answers.

**Choice:** OpenAI `gpt-6.2-sol` for everything, with medium reasoning effort.

**Why.** Prepaid credit was available on OpenAI. Using one model keeps behavior predictable and the evaluation results meaningful (a two-model setup doubles the combinations to test). The model is isolated in `app/agent/llm_client.py`, so switching provider means rewriting that one file. Measured cost is about 0.013 USD per answer.

## D3. Data storage: SQLite in the repository

**Options considered:** Postgres, DuckDB, flat files (CSV or Parquet), SQLite.

**Choice:** SQLite, with the built database committed to git.

**Why.** The service only reads data; all writes happen in the offline build. The data is about 49 MB after compaction. SQLite needs no server, works the same on a laptop and in a container, and the committed file means a reviewer can run the app without downloading anything or waiting for a build. DuckDB would also work but adds a dependency without a real benefit at this size. Postgres becomes the right choice when several processes write (shared conversation history, alert history) or when the hub network grows very large.

## D4. How to measure risk (the most important decision)

This went through four versions. Each change was triggered by evidence, not by preference.

**Version 1: weather thresholds with hand-picked hazard weights.** Count days above thresholds (heavy snow, extreme heat, high wind and so on) and combine them with weights such as winter 0.25. Rejected by the user and by us: the weights are opinions, and changing them changes the ranking.

**Version 2: disruption days without weights.** Count every day that crosses any threshold, all days equal. Rejected after the first results: Phoenix and Las Vegas ranked at the top because temperatures over 38 C are normal there (about 106 days a year in Phoenix) and the local infrastructure is built for it. A fixed national threshold does not mean the same thing everywhere, and a hot day counted the same as a hurricane day.

**Version 3: FEMA building loss as a severity weight.** Rejected: property damage is not the same as operational disruption of a distribution hub, and the National Risk Index loss numbers are dominated by how much property exists in a county, not by how often the weather is bad.

**Version 4 (current): NWS warnings for frequency, FEMA major-disaster declarations for severity.**

- National Weather Service warning criteria are set by each local office, so a warning means "dangerous for this place". This fixed the Phoenix problem without us choosing any threshold.
- FEMA declarations show how often a warning day became an actual disaster. The share of warning days inside a declared disaster gives each hazard its severity from data: about 46% for hurricanes, 17% for floods, 5% for winter, 4% for thunderstorms and 0% for heat. Nobody chose these numbers.
- The primary measure is disaster-level days per year (warning days times severity share). Warning days per year are always reported next to it, so a hub with frequent but rarely catastrophic weather does not look safe.

**Thought process on heat.** Heat getting zero disaster-level days looked wrong at first. We checked: FEMA did not declare a single heat disaster in our 30-year window. Rather than invent a severity for heat, we kept the data result and made the system say clearly that this means "no evidence of disaster-level heat", while still reporting heat warning days.

## D5. Rules to keep the method honest

- **No parameter tuned to a ranking.** Every threshold, radius and pattern is in `app/scoring/params.yaml` with its reason. When a value needed a test, the test was decided before looking at the ranking it would produce. For example, the 150 km hurricane radius and 50 km storm radius were accepted because rankings stayed stable across nearby radii (rank correlation 0.83 to 0.98).
- **No hub-specific fixes.** When a single hub looked wrong, we looked for the general cause. Two examples:
  - Phoenix had 758 flash-flood warnings because Maricopa County is huge. The general fix: storm-based warnings count only when the warning polygon contains the hub. Phoenix dropped to 31, and every other large county was corrected the same way.
  - Some winter disasters were missing because FEMA filed them as "Severe Storm". The general fix: match declarations by type or by title keywords, with snowmelt and ice jams excluded from winter because they are floods.
- **No use of our own prior knowledge as data.** Expected answers in the evaluation are computed by calling the tools, never typed in by hand.

## D6. Tiers and uncertainty

**Tiers:** thirds of the network (High, Elevated, Low). Fixed cut-offs (for example "over 1 day is high") would be arbitrary because the measure is new and has no external scale. Thirds are simple to explain and always relative to the client's own network.

**Uncertainty:** exact Poisson ranges for rates, exact binomial ranges for shares, and a conservative combination for disaster-level days. We chose conservative over precise because overstating certainty is worse for an investment decision than a wide range.

**Confidence label:** rule-based (station distance, station completeness, how much modeled data was used), so the same data always gives the same label.

## D7. Station data first, model data as backup

Weather statistics questions ("what share of days in Denver had snowfall last year?") are answered from the nearest major airport station (NOAA GHCN-Daily), and Open-Meteo reanalysis fills missing days. Reanalysis alone smooths extremes and missed real snow days in our checks; stations measure what actually happened but have gaps. The answer always says which source was used.

## D8. Places that are not hubs

**Options considered:** refuse; use the nearest hub; run a live assessment for any address; recommend a similar nearby hub.

**Choice:** recommend a stand-in hub and ask before analyzing it.

**Why.** Refusing is unhelpful, and the nearest hub can be misleading (for Charleston, SC the nearest hub is inland Charlotte, while coastal Jacksonville has the matching hurricane and flood profile). A live assessment for any address would be the best answer but needs a different data pipeline; it is listed as future work. The recommendation weighs hazard similarity (80%) above distance (20%), because the purpose is to find a hub with similar weather, and distance mainly breaks ties.

**Ambiguous names and nicknames.** We first considered adding ZIP codes and a nickname table. We decided this was more than the assignment needs: the model converts nicknames to official names (and says so in the answer), and ambiguity is decided from Census population data (one match over 50,000 people wins, otherwise ask). The evaluation found that the model sometimes decided "Springfield is ambiguous" on its own without calling the tool; the prompt now requires the tool call so the decision comes from data.

**Coverage limit.** Instead of listing excluded states, the limit is the widest gap between neighboring hubs in the network (622 km today). This excludes Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico automatically and adapts if the client adds hubs.

## D9. Contract between model and code

- **Strict tool schemas** generated from Pydantic models, with fixed lists for hub ids and regions.
- **A fixed final answer format** (JSON) instead of free text, so code can check it.
- **Number tracing in code.** The first version asked the model to list every figure with its source. It made answers about 60% longer and slower, and it relied on the model to describe itself. We moved tracing into code: it searches the tool outputs for each number in the text. Output tokens dropped by 45%, and the check became stricter.
- **One retry, then a visible warning.** We chose not to hide or silently drop a failed answer; the user sees what could not be verified.
- **Text cleanup in code.** The prompt asks for plain writing without dashes or ellipses, and code removes any that slip through, so the result does not depend on the model following the style rule.

## D10. Answer length

We considered shortening answers to reduce latency. The user preferred complete answers, because analysts use them for investment decisions. We kept the information and reduced latency in other ways (code-side tracing, cached prompt, trimmed history). Average time is about 10 seconds per answer.

## D11. User interface

- **Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript** without a framework or build step. The UI is small, and a reviewer can read it directly. Libraries (markdown rendering, HTML sanitizing) and the font are stored in the repository, so the page works without external CDNs.
- **Client view by default, developer view on request.** Early versions showed tool traces and token counts to everyone. The audience is a logistics analyst, so technical details moved behind a developer toggle, which is still available for the demonstration.
- **Seasonal outlook** was added because "what should we prepare for this month?" is a practical question for operations, and it reuses the same warning data. It is labeled as historical frequency, not a forecast.

## D12. Protecting a public deployment
