level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. 158:- Store every county (not just hub counties). NRI scores are national percentiles (0–100). Missing values (e.g. no coastal flood inland) are stored as 0 and the substitution is recorded.
174:- **HURDAT2** (NOAA NHC, Atlantic + NE Pacific): 6-hourly storm positions and winds. Window **1950–2025** (reliable from aircraft reconnaissance). Table `storm_tracks`.
181:- **Station rule:** nearest `USW` (major airport/first-order) station within 40 km whose 1996–2025 PRCP and TMAX records are ≥ 90% complete; otherwise the next nearest. Chosen from NOAA's station inventory, not by hand. Table `hub_stations` (station id, name, distance, completeness).
182:- **Data:** daily PRCP, SNOW, TMAX, TMIN, WSF5 (peak 5-second gust), and observed weather types WT03 (thunder), WT04 (ice pellets), WT05 (hail), WT06 (glaze), WT17 (freezing rain), **1996–2025** (30-year window). Source: NCEI Access Data Service (no token). Table `station_daily`.
183:- **Combination:** per day and variable, station value if present, else Open-Meteo (2016–2025 only); every value carries its source. Share of gap-filled values reported per hub.
184:- Caveats: weather-type flags are recorded inconsistently (a missing flag doesn't prove nothing happened); the airport can be 10–25 km from the city center.
187:- **NWS warnings** (Iowa Environmental Mesonet VTEC archive, by hub county + forecast zone from the NWS points API), warnings only, 2006–2025. Locally calibrated: a warning means conditions expected to be dangerous *for that place* (fixes fixed-threshold bias, e.g. Phoenix 106 days ≥ 38 °C vs ~3 Excessive Heat Warnings/yr). Phenomena → hazards: winter (WS, BZ, IS, LE), flood (FF, FA, CF; river-gauge FL excluded), convective/wind (SV, TO, HW, EW, DS), hurricane (HU, TR, SS), heat (EH, XH).
188:- **FEMA disaster declarations** (OpenFEMA), major disasters (DR), weather incident types, 1996–2025.
199:## Phase 3 — Metrics & deterministic scoring engine (≈2.5 h, no LLM cost)
206:| `ice_day` | **Changed:** the Open-Meteo daily archive never emits freezing codes (56/57/66/67) or thunderstorm codes (95–99), checked over all data. Proxy instead: precip ≥ 2 mm, tmin < 0 °C, tmax 0–3 °C, and a liquid part (precip − 0.7 × snowfall_cm) ≥ 1 mm. Crude, so the ice signal leans on NRI ice-storm frequency |
215:- Annual averages over 2016–2025 per hub, plus per-year values (so "last year" questions work).
218:### 3.3 Sub-scores (0–100) (`scoring/engine.py`)
226:| Hurricane | coastal_flood | **HURDAT2 storm rate within radius (1950–2025)** + damaging_wind_days | to set in Phase 3 (rule 1) |
228:| Convective | — (FEMA kept as cross-check) | **SPC tornado / hail / wind rates within radius (1996+)** + thunder days, damaging_wind_days | to set in Phase 3 (rule 1) |

235:- Tiers: High ≥ 60, Elevated 40–60, Low < 40.

259:| `get_methodology` | — | KPI definitions, severity shares with ranges, warning/incident type mappings, data sources, assumptions and limitations |

import re
import sys

sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
root = r"C:\Users\97254\Downloads\Moveo_Assignment\weather-risk-agent"
files = sys.argv[1:]

def fix_line(line: str) -> str:
    if line.lstrip().startswith("#"):
        line = line.replace(" — ", ": ", 1)
    line = line.replace(" — ", ", ").replace("—", ", ")
    line = re.sub(r"(\d)\s*–\s*(\d)", r"\1 to \2", line)
    line = line.replace(" – ", ", ").replace("–", "-")
    reps = {"→": "->", "←": "<-", "≥": ">=", "≤": "<=", "≈": "about ", "~": "about ", "°C": " C", "°": "",
            "≠": "is not", "×": "x", "−": "-", "…": "...", "✓": "yes", "✗": "no", "±": "+/-",
            "├── ": "  ", "└── ": "  ", "│   ": "  ", "│": " ", "“": '"', "”": '"', "’": "'", "‘": "'"}
    for a, b in reps.items():
        line = line.replace(a, b)
    line = line.replace("...", ".")  # no ellipses
    line = re.sub(r"about  +", "about ", line)
    return line

for f in files:
    p = root + "\\" + f
    text = open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()
    in_code = False
    out = []
    for line in text.split("\n"):
        out.append(fix_line(line))
    new = "\n".join(out)
    open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n").write(new)
    left = sorted({c for c in new if ord(c) > 127})
    print(f, "remaining non-ascii:", left)

- Hazard prefixes: `WNTW, ISTM, CWAV, HRCN, CFLD, IFLD` (Inland Flooding, which replaces the older Riverine Flooding), `TRND, HAIL, SWND, HWAV`.

- **Decision: use annualized event frequency (`<HAZ>_AFREQ`), not the risk score.** The NRI hazard risk score scales with exposed property and population, so big urban counties score high on everything (Dallas County about 99 for winter weather; Hennepin about 99.6 for tornado). For a logistics hub, how often a hazard occurs is what matters. We store `afreq`, a national percentile of it (`freq_pctl`, 0 when the hazard never occurs), plus `risk_score` and the loss-rate percentile for reference.
-- Known caveat: percentiles flatten the low end (e.g. Phoenix's hurricane percentile is ~50 though its frequency is ~26x lower than Miami's). Phase 3 may scale hurricane by raw frequency instead.

content.text:
I've written the documentation, and it's committed and pushed (048359d). It has no AI-style symbols: all four docs contain only plain ASCII characters, which I checked with a script.

- **[DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md)** covers the architecture (with a diagram and the steps a chat request goes through) and the repository structure. It also covers:
  - the data sources, why we use SQLite and when Postgres would be the better choice;
  - how risk is measured and how that method changed through four versions;
  - places that aren't hubs, and the contract between the model and the code;
  - the API and interface, testing and evaluation results, assumptions and limitations, and what we didn't build.
- **[DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md)** has 13 decisions. Each one lists the options, the choice and the reasoning. It includes the risk-measure versions we dropped after looking at the data (Phoenix ranking first under fixed thresholds, heat having zero disaster-level days) and the rule that fixes must be general, never hub-specific.
- **[README.md](README.md)** now starts with a plain explanation of what the app does, then a table linking the docs. It also explains how to open the web app and the developer view, and adds the outlook endpoint to the API table.

content.text:
The voice feature needs no backend changes and costs nothing to run. It uses the browser's built-in Web Speech API, so all of it lives in `web/app.js`, `index.html` and `styles.css`.

## How it would work

**1. Speaking a question (mic button next to Send)**
- The browser's speech recognition turns your speech into text. Chrome, Edge and Safari support it; Firefox doesn't.
- **If the browser doesn't support it, the mic button is hidden.** Nothing looks broken.
- **Click the mic:**
  - It turns red and pulses while it listens, and the words appear in the input box as you speak.
  - It stops when you stop talking or click again.
  - It's set to US English.
- **I recommend the text is not sent automatically.** It stays in the box so you can check it and press Enter. Speech recognition sometimes gets place names wrong ("Wichita", "Fargo"), and a wrong hub name would give a confident answer to the wrong question.
- **Errors get a plain message**, for example "Microphone access was blocked" or "Didn't catch that, try again".

**2. Read-aloud (a speaker toggle in the header)**
- When it's on, each new answer is read aloud by the browser's built-in speech. Every modern browser supports this, Firefox included.
- **It reads a cleaned version of the answer:**
  - the visible text without markdown symbols;
  - tables read row by row;
  - the sources and technical sections skipped.
- **Reading stops** when you ask a new question, start a new chat or turn the toggle off.
- The browser remembers the setting.

**Two things to know**
- **The mic needs a secure page.** `localhost` counts as secure, and so does the Render URL (https), so both will work.
- **Chrome sends the recorded audio to Google's speech service to transcribe it.** That's normal for this feature, but I'll mention it in the docs as a privacy note. A production version could use an in-house speech model instead.

## How we test it

**What I can check myself in the built-in browser:**
- The buttons render, look right in light and dark mode, and work at phone width.
- **Unsupported browser:** I remove the speech API from the page and confirm the mic button is hidden.
- **Mic flow with a fake microphone:** I replace the speech API with a stub that "hears" a sample question. Then I check:
  - the text fills the input box;
  - the button state changes;
  - an error event shows the right message.
- **Read-aloud:** I replace the speech output with a stub and confirm that:
  - it's called with clean text (no `**`, `|` or `#`);
  - it isn't called when the toggle is off;
  - it stops on a new question.
- **The existing 125 tests** still pass, since the server isn't touched.

**What only you can test (a real microphone and speakers):**
- In Chrome or Edge, open `http://127.0.0.1:8000` and click the mic. Allow microphone access when asked.
- Say two of the assignment questions, for example "Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter disruption?" and "Why is the Dallas hub high?". Check the text before sending.
- Turn on read-aloud and listen to one answer. Then ask another question while it's speaking and confirm the first one stops.
- Optionally open it in Firefox: the mic should be hidden and read-aloud should still work.
- After the deploy, repeat the mic test once on the Render URL, so we know it works over https.

It's about 45 minutes, as planned. Should I go ahead with the "check it before sending" behavior, or would you prefer the question to send automatically when you stop speaking?

lines: - **Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript** without a framework or build step. The UI is small, and a reviewer can read it directly. Libraries (markdown rendering, HTML sanitizing) and the font are stored in the repository, so the page works without external CDNs.

- **Client view by default, developer view on request.** Early versions showed tool traces and token counts to everyone. The audience is a logistics analyst, so technical details moved behind a developer toggle, which is still available for the demonstration.

+- **Voice in the browser, not on the server.** The Web Speech API gives speech input and read-aloud with no new dependency, no server change and no cost, which fit the time left. A server-side speech model would give consistent quality across browsers and keep audio in-house, but it adds cost and a new service. Spoken questions are placed in the input box instead of being sent automatically, because a misheard hub name would lead to a confident answer about the wrong place.

- **Seasonal outlook** was added because "what should we prepare for this month?" is a practical question for operations, and it reuses the same warning data. It is labeled as historical frequency, not a forecast.
-| Web UI (`web/`) | Chat, seasonal outlook, leaderboard, hub details, methodology. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step | FastAPI over HTTP/JSON |
+| Web UI (`web/`) | Chat (typed or spoken), read-aloud, seasonal outlook, leaderboard, hub details, methodology. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step | FastAPI over HTTP/JSON |
| FastAPI (`app/api/main.py`) | Chat endpoint, data endpoints, health check, access code, rate limit, daily spend cap | Agent, tools |

| Agent (`app/agent/agent.py`) | Runs the conversation: sends the question to the model, executes the tools it asks for, validates the final answer | OpenAI (through `llm_client.py` only), tools, validator |
| Tools (`app/tools/`) | Eight deterministic functions: rank, compare, explain a hub, weather statistics, seasonal outlook, methodology, list hubs, find a stand-in hub | SQLite |

**Protection for a public URL**: an access code on every `/api/*` call, 10 chat messages per minute per IP address, and a daily OpenAI spend cap (3 USD by default, adjustable at runtime) after which chat answers with a clear message while the data views keep working.
+**Voice**: voice runs entirely in the browser through the Web Speech API, so the server, the agent and the cost are unchanged.

+- *Speaking a question*: the microphone button turns speech into text in the input box. The text is not sent automatically: speech recognition sometimes mishears place names, and a wrong hub name would produce a confident answer to the wrong question, so the user checks the text and presses Enter. The button is hidden in browsers without speech recognition (for example Firefox), and errors such as a blocked microphone get a plain message.

+- *Reading answers aloud*: a "Read aloud" switch reads each new answer, and a speaker button on every answer reads that one. The spoken text is built from the displayed answer: one sentence per paragraph, list item and table row, without markdown symbols, and "/yr" is read as "per year". It is spoken a few sentences at a time because Chrome stops long utterances after about 15 seconds. Reading stops when a new question is asked or a new chat starts.
+- *Privacy*: in Chrome, speech recognition sends the audio to Google's speech service. A production deployment that must keep audio in-house would use a self-hosted speech model instead.

**Client view and developer view**: by default the interface shows what a client needs (the answer, a confidence badge, "Sources and reliability" with a confirmation that all figures were checked against the data, plain-language evidence in the hub panel). Tool calls, field-level number tracing, tokens and cost are available in a developer view (Methodology, "Show technical details", or `?dev=1`) for demonstrations.

- Ask questions in a chat, for example "Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter disruption?", "Compare Miami and Houston for hurricanes and flooding", "What percentage of days in Denver last year had snowfall?" or "Why is the Dallas hub high?".
- See this month's seasonal outlook (which hubs historically face the most disruption in the current month).
- Browse the leaderboard of all 47 hubs by hazard and region, and open any hub to see the evidence behind its score.
+- Use voice: click the microphone to speak a question (Chrome, Edge and Safari), check the text and press Enter. Turn on "Read aloud" to hear answers, or click the speaker icon on any answer.

content.text:
Voice is in the app and pushed (90fbe74). It runs entirely in the browser, so the server and the cost are unchanged. Every flow passed my tests with fake speech objects in the browser, and the 125 unit tests still pass; nothing has been tried with a real microphone or speakers yet.

**What it does:**
- **Mic button** (next to Send):
  - What you say appears in the input box while you speak, and is not sent until you press Enter.
  - A second click stops listening, and speaking again adds to the text already there.
  - It's hidden in browsers without speech recognition, such as Firefox.
  - Errors get a plain message, for example "Microphone access is blocked…" or "Didn't catch that…".
- **Read aloud switch** (header): reads each new answer. The browser remembers the setting, and it starts off.
- **Speaker button on every answer**: reads that answer, and a second click stops it.
- Reading stops when you send a new question or start a new chat.

**One bug found and fixed:** the first version split sentences at every period, so "1.91" was read as "91". It now splits only at real sentence ends.

**What I checked with fakes:**
- the mic's listening state and its text filling the box without sending;
- adding to existing text;
- the error messages;
- sending while listening (it stops listening, and late results are ignored);
- read-aloud being off by default;
- the per-answer button, and spoken text without markdown symbols (tables read row by row);
- the switch, and stopping on a new question or new chat;
- the mic hidden when the browser doesn't support it.

I also added a voice section to DESIGN.md, including the privacy note that Chrome sends the audio to Google's speech service, a voice decision in DECISIONS.md and a line in the README.

**To test it yourself (about 2 minutes, in Chrome or Edge):**
1. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 and click the mic. Allow microphone access when asked.
2. Say "Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter disruption?", check the text, then press Enter.
3. Click the speaker icon on the answer, or turn on Read aloud and ask "Why is the Dallas hub high?".

# Weather Risk Intelligence Agent: production image.
# The database (data/risk.db) is part of the repository, so the image needs no data download at build or start time.
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY app ./app
COPY web ./web
COPY data/hubs.yaml data/risk.db ./data/

# Run as a non-root user.
RUN useradd --create-home appuser && chown -R appuser /app
USER appuser

# Render sets PORT; 8000 is the local default.
ENV PORT=8000
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=20s \
    CMD python -c "import os, urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen(f'http://127.0.0.1:{os.environ[\"PORT\"]}/health', timeout=4)"

content.text:
Yes, pick the final code now and enter it straight into Render. A few points:

- **The Render code and your `.env` code are separate.** Render never reads your `.env`; it only uses what you type into its dashboard. You don't need to change `.env` at all, since that's only for your local copy.
- **Choose the code you'll give the reviewers.** Make it easy to type from an email but not guessable, for example two unrelated words and a number. Avoid your name, "moveo" or "weather".
- **Changing it later is still easy if you need to.** In Render, open the service, go to **Environment**, edit the value and save. The service restarts in about a minute. Nothing in the repo changes, so this doesn't count as changing your submission.
- **Where reviewers get the code:** put it in your submission message next to the URL, not in the README or anywhere in the repo, because the repo is public.

Use the same approach for `ADMIN_TOKEN`: make it long and random, and keep it to yourself. It's only for raising the daily budget during the demo if needed.

content.text:
Yes, keep them different.

- **The access code gets shared.** Reviewers get it, and anyone they forward the email to has it too. All it lets someone do is use the app, within the rate limit and the daily budget.
- **The admin token stays with you.** It can change the daily spending cap. If it matched the access code, anyone who can use the app could also raise the limit and spend your OpenAI credit.

Make the admin token long and random, for example a 32-character random string from a password manager. You'll never type it into the app; you'd only use it in a single command during the demo if you need more budget. Keep it in your password manager or local `.env`, and don't put it in the submission email.

content.text:
Yes, that's fine. At 32 characters, even keyboard mashing is long enough that nobody will guess it. Two small tips:

- **Use only letters and numbers.** The token goes in an HTTP header, and spaces, quotes or symbols like `"`, `'` or `$` can break it when you paste it into a command.
- **Save it somewhere** (your password manager or the local `.env`) before you paste it into Render, because Render hides it afterwards.

If you'd rather not invent one, this command prints a random 32-character token you can copy:

```powershell
-join ((48..57) + (65..90) + (97..122) | Get-Random -Count 32 | ForEach-Object { [char]$_ })
```

content.text:
It's not a bug. The layout changes with screen width:

- **Narrow screens** (phones, or the small preview pane you saw earlier): there's no room for a side column, so the leaderboard is hidden behind the "Leaderboard" button in the header.
- **Wide screens** (your Chrome window now): the page has room, so the leaderboard shows as a fixed column on the right, and the button is hidden.

I can make it switchable on wide screens too, with the "Leaderboard" button always in the header. The open question is what a first-time visitor sees:

- **Open by default, with a button to hide it (my recommendation).** The ranking is the core of the assignment ("rank hubs by exposure"), so a reviewer sees it immediately. Anyone who wants more room for the chat can hide it, and the browser remembers that choice.
- **Closed by default, opened with the button.** The chat and outlook get the full width, but a reviewer has to discover the button to see the ranking.

Either way it's about 15 minutes, including a check at desktop and phone widths and a push, which redeploys Render automatically.

"""Scoring engine.

KPIs (no chosen hazard weights):
- Routine disruption days/yr per hazard = days covered by an NWS warning for that hazard at the
  hub (county or forecast zone), 2006-2025. NWS criteria are set locally, so a warning means
  conditions expected to be dangerous *for that place*.
- Severity share per hazard = share of warning days (pooled over all hubs) that fall inside a
  FEMA major-disaster incident period of a matching type in the hub's county.
- Severe disruption days/yr = sum over hazards of routine days x severity share
  -> the primary ranking (resilience investment targets severe events).
Evidence kept for explanations: measured threshold days (station data 1996-2025), HURDAT2 storm
counts and named storms, SPC report days, descriptive climate metrics.

Usage:
    python -m app.scoring.engine --print
"""

import argparse
import json
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from app.db import get_connection
from app.scoring import metrics as m
from app.scoring.params import get_params

HAZARDS = ["winter", "flood", "convective", "hurricane", "heat"]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- pure functions


def composite_days(hazard_days: dict[str, float], day_costs: dict[str, float] | None = None) -> float:
    costs = day_costs or get_params()["scoring"]["default_day_costs"]
    return float(sum((hazard_days.get(h) or 0.0) * costs.get(h, 1) for h in HAZARDS))


def assign_tiers(values: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    """Top / middle / bottom third of hubs (ties broken by hub id for determinism)."""
    order = values.reset_index().sort_values([values.name, values.index.name], ascending=[False, True])
    labels = np.empty(len(order), dtype=object)
    for label, idx in zip(("High", "Elevated", "Low"), np.array_split(np.arange(len(order)), 3)):
        labels[idx] = label
    return pd.Series(labels, index=order[values.index.name].to_numpy()).reindex(values.index)


def confidence(st_info: dict | None, infos: dict, rules: dict) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
    reasons = []
    if st_info is None:
        reasons.append("no qualifying weather station; modeled data only")
    else:
        if st_info["distance_km"] > rules["station_far_km"]:
            reasons.append(f"station is {st_info['distance_km']:.0f} km from the hub")
        if rules["gust_not_measured"] and not st_info["gust_measured"]:
            reasons.append("no measured gusts or weather events at the station (modeled gusts used; ice not observed)")
    if rules["variable_from_open_meteo"]:
        fell_back = [v for v, i in infos.items() if i.source == "open_meteo" and v != "gust_kmh"]
        if fell_back:
            reasons.append(f"modeled (Open-Meteo 2016-2025) data used for: {', '.join(fell_back)}")
    level = ["high", "medium", "low"][min(len(reasons), 2)]
    return level, reasons


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- per hub (pass 1)


def _event_row(conn, hub_id, hazard, radius):
    return conn.execute("SELECT events, rate_per_year, rate_lo, rate_hi, first_year, last_year, details_json "
                        "FROM hub_event_rates WHERE hub_id=? AND hazard=? AND radius_km=?",
                        (hub_id, hazard, radius)).fetchone()


def hub_evidence(conn: sqlite3.Connection, hub_id: str) -> dict:
    """Everything for one hub except the pooled severity shares."""
    p = get_params()
    sp, ep, wp = p["scoring"], p["event_rates"], p["warnings"]
    level = ep["confidence_level"]

    # Routine disruption: NWS warning days.
    ugc = conn.execute("SELECT ugc, kind, timezone FROM hub_ugc WHERE hub_id=?", (hub_id,)).fetchall()
    tz = ugc[0][2] if ugc else "UTC"
    codes = [u[0] for u in ugc] + [f"POINT:{hub_id}"]   # zone/county products + polygons containing the hub
    warns = pd.read_sql(f"SELECT phenomena, issue, expire FROM nws_warnings WHERE ugc IN "
                        f"({','.join('?' * len(codes))})", conn, params=codes)
    wdays = m.warning_days(warns, tz, wp["phenomena"], (wp["first_year"], wp["last_year"]))
    n_days = len(pd.date_range(f"{wp['first_year']}-01-01", f"{wp['last_year']}-12-31"))

    # Evidence: measured threshold days (station-first daily data).
    series, infos, wt, st_info = m.load_hub_daily(conn, hub_id)
    torn = _event_row(conn, hub_id, "tornado", ep["default_radius_km"]["convective"])
    tornado_dates = set(json.loads(torn[6]).get("dates", [])) if torn else set()
    flags = m.disruption_flags(series, wt, tornado_dates, sp["thresholds"])

    hazards = {}
    for h in HAZARDS:
        r = m.rate_with_interval(len(wdays[h]), n_days, level)
        hazards[h] = {"warning_days_per_year": r["per_year"], "warning_days_range": [r["lo"], r["hi"]],
                      "warning_days_total": r["events"], "warning_window": [wp["first_year"], wp["last_year"]],
                      "warning_types": wp["phenomena"][h]}
        if h in flags:
            t = m.summarize_flags(flags[h], level)
            var = {"winter": "snow_cm", "flood": "precip_mm", "convective": "gust_kmh", "heat": "tmax_c"}[h]
            hazards[h]["threshold_days"] = {"per_year": t["per_year"], "range": [t["lo"], t["hi"]],
                                            "rule": sp["disruption_rules"][h], "source": infos[var].source,
                                            "window": list(infos[var].window)}

    hr = _event_row(conn, hub_id, "hurricane_days", ep["default_radius_km"]["hurricane"])
    storms = _event_row(conn, hub_id, "hurricane", ep["default_radius_km"]["hurricane"])
    hu = _event_row(conn, hub_id, "hurricane_strength", ep["default_radius_km"]["hurricane"])
    hazards["hurricane"]["storm_record"] = {
        "radius_km": ep["default_radius_km"]["hurricane"], "window": [storms[4], storms[5]],
        "storm_days_per_year": hr[1], "storms_per_decade": storms[1] * 10,
        "storms_per_decade_range": [storms[2] * 10, storms[3] * 10],
        "hurricane_strength_per_decade": hu[1] * 10, "p_storm_within_10y": float(1 - np.exp(-storms[1] * 10)),
        "notable_storms": json.loads(hu[6])["notable_storms"] or json.loads(storms[6])["notable_storms"]}

    desc = {}
    for name, s in m.descriptive_flags(series, wt, sp["descriptive_thresholds"]).items():
        st = m.summarize_flags(s, level)
        desc[name] = {"per_year": st["per_year"], "range": [st["lo"], st["hi"]], "years_observed": st["years"]}
    desc["max_3day_precip_mm"] = {"value": m.max_3day_precip_mean(series["precip_mm"])}
    snow = series["snow_cm"].copy()
    snow.index = pd.to_datetime(snow.index)
    desc["annual_snowfall_cm"] = {"value": float(snow.groupby(snow.index.year).sum(min_count=300).mean())}
    for h in ("tornado", "hail", "wind"):
        r = _event_row(conn, hub_id, h, ep["default_radius_km"]["convective"])
        desc[f"{h}_report_days"] = {"per_year": r[1], "range": [r[2], r[3]],
                                    "radius_km": ep["default_radius_km"]["convective"], "window": [r[4], r[5]]}

    conf, reasons = confidence(st_info, infos, sp["confidence_rules"])
    return {"hub_id": hub_id, "hazards": hazards, "descriptive": desc, "station": st_info,
            "variables": {k: vars(v) for k, v in infos.items()}, "nws_ugc": [u[0] for u in ugc],
            "confidence": conf, "confidence_reasons": reasons, "_warning_dates": wdays}


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- severity shares (pooled)


def declarations_for_hazard(decl: pd.DataFrame, hazard: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Declarations matching a hazard by FEMA incident type OR by title (FEMA often files winter
    disasters under 'Severe Storm' / 'Flood'); patterns in params.yaml -> declarations."""
    dp = get_params()["declarations"]
    by_type = decl["incident_type"].isin(dp["incident_types"][hazard])
    pattern = dp.get("title_patterns", {}).get(hazard)
    by_title = decl["title"].fillna("").str.contains(pattern, case=False, regex=True) if pattern else False
    return decl[by_type | by_title]


def severity_shares(conn: sqlite3.Connection, evidence: dict[str, dict]) -> dict[str, dict]:
    p = get_params()
    decl = pd.read_sql("SELECT county_fips, incident_type, title, begin_date, end_date FROM fema_declarations", conn)
    county = dict(conn.execute("SELECT id, county_fips FROM hubs").fetchall())
    k, n = {h: 0 for h in HAZARDS}, {h: 0 for h in HAZARDS}
    for hub_id, ev in evidence.items():
        dc = decl[decl["county_fips"] == county[hub_id]]
        for h in HAZARDS:
            dates = ev["_warning_dates"][h]
            inc = declarations_for_hazard(dc, h)
            k[h] += m.dates_in_incidents(dates, inc)
            n[h] += len(dates)
    return {h: m.share_with_interval(k[h], n[h], p["event_rates"]["confidence_level"]) for h in HAZARDS}


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- all hubs


def score_all(conn: sqlite3.Connection, day_costs: dict | None = None, store: bool = True) -> pd.DataFrame:
    p = get_params()
    hub_ids = [r[0] for r in conn.execute("SELECT id FROM hubs ORDER BY id")]
    evidence = {h: hub_evidence(conn, h) for h in hub_ids}
    shares = severity_shares(conn, evidence)

    rows = {}
    for h, ev in evidence.items():
        ev.pop("_warning_dates")
        severe = {}
        for z in HAZARDS:
            hz = ev["hazards"][z]
            hz["severity_share"] = shares[z]
            hz["severe_days_per_year"] = (hz["warning_days_per_year"] or 0.0) * shares[z]["share"]
            severe[z] = hz["severe_days_per_year"]
        routine = {z: ev["hazards"][z]["warning_days_per_year"] or 0.0 for z in HAZARDS}
        rows[h] = {**severe, "composite": composite_days(severe, day_costs),
                   "routine_total": composite_days(routine, day_costs), "confidence": ev["confidence"]}
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
    df.index.name = "hub_id"
    for c in HAZARDS + ["composite", "routine_total"]:
        df[c] = df[c].astype(float)
    df["tier"] = assign_tiers(df["composite"])
    df["rank"] = df["composite"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
    df["routine_rank"] = df["routine_total"].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)

    if store:
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds")
        version = f"{p['scoring']['kpi_version']}/params-{p['params_version']}"
        conn.executemany(
            "INSERT INTO risk_scores (hub_id, computed_at, scoring_version, composite, winter, hurricane, flood, "
            "convective, heat, tier, details_json) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
            [(h, now, version, float(r.composite), float(r.winter), float(r.hurricane), float(r.flood),
              float(r.convective), float(r.heat), r.tier,
              json.dumps({**evidence[h], "rank": int(r["rank"]), "of": len(df),
                          "routine_total": float(r.routine_total), "routine_rank": int(r.routine_rank)},
                         default=float))
             for h, r in df.iterrows()])
        conn.execute("DELETE FROM hub_metrics")
        conn.executemany(
            "INSERT INTO hub_metrics (hub_id, metric, period, value) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
            [(h, name, f"{p['scoring']['window'][0]}-{p['scoring']['window'][1]}", v.get("per_year", v.get("value")))
             for h, ev in evidence.items() for name, v in ev["descriptive"].items()])
        conn.commit()
    return df.sort_values("composite", ascending=False)


def latest_breakdown(conn: sqlite3.Connection, hub_id: str) -> dict | None:
    row = conn.execute("SELECT computed_at, scoring_version, composite, tier, details_json FROM risk_scores "
                       "WHERE hub_id = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1", (hub_id,)).fetchone()
    if not row:
        return None
    d = json.loads(row[4])
    total = row[2] or 1.0
    d["severe_days_per_year"], d["tier"], d["computed_at"], d["scoring_version"] = row[2], row[3], row[0], row[1]
    d["contributions"] = sorted(
        [{"hazard": h, "severe_days_per_year": d["hazards"][h]["severe_days_per_year"],
          "share_of_total": d["hazards"][h]["severe_days_per_year"] / total if total else 0.0,
          "warning_days_per_year": d["hazards"][h]["warning_days_per_year"],
          "severity_share": d["hazards"][h]["severity_share"]["share"]} for h in HAZARDS],
        key=lambda x: -x["severe_days_per_year"])
    return d


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--print", action="store_true", help="print the ranking")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    conn = get_connection()
    df = score_all(conn)
    if args.print:
        pd.set_option("display.width", 170)
        print(df[["rank", "tier", "composite"] + HAZARDS + ["routine_total", "routine_rank", "confidence"]]
              .round(2).to_string())
        r = json.loads(conn.execute("SELECT details_json FROM risk_scores ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0])
        print("\nSeverity shares:", {h: round(r["hazards"][h]["severity_share"]["share"], 3) for h in HAZARDS})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Daily hub weather (station first, Open-Meteo as backup) and day-based metrics.

Pure functions (combine_variable, disruption_flags, rate_with_interval, descriptive flags)
take pandas objects and are unit-tested on synthetic data. load_hub_daily() wraps the
database.
"""

import sqlite3
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import chi2

from app.scoring.params import get_params

DAYS_PER_YEAR = 365.25

# variable -> (station_daily column, daily_weather (Open-Meteo) column)
VARIABLES = {
    "precip_mm": ("prcp_mm", "precip_mm"),
    "snow_cm": ("snow_cm", "snowfall_cm"),
    "tmax_c": ("tmax_c", "tmax_c"),
    "tmin_c": ("tmin_c", "tmin_c"),
    "gust_kmh": ("gust_kmh", "wind_gust_kmh"),
}
WT_FLAGS = ["wt_thunder", "wt_ice_pellets", "wt_hail", "wt_glaze", "wt_freezing_rain"]


@dataclass
class VariableInfo:
    source: str              # station | station+open_meteo | open_meteo
    window: tuple[str, str]  # dates actually used
    coverage: float          # share of window days with a value
    filled_share: float      # share of used values that came from Open-Meteo
    notes: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


def combine_variable(station: pd.Series, open_meteo: pd.Series, window: tuple[str, str],
                     om_window: tuple[str, str], min_coverage: float,
                     station_usable: bool = True) -> tuple[pd.Series, VariableInfo]:
    """Station value where present, else Open-Meteo. If coverage stays below min_coverage
    (or the station can't be used for this variable), use Open-Meteo alone over its window."""
    days = pd.date_range(*window).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    st = station.reindex(days) if station_usable else pd.Series(np.nan, index=days)
    om = open_meteo.reindex(days)
    combined = st.combine_first(om)
    coverage = float(combined.notna().mean())
    if station_usable and coverage >= min_coverage:
        filled = float((st.isna() & om.notna()).sum() / max(combined.notna().sum(), 1))
        src = "station" if filled == 0 else "station+open_meteo"
        return combined, VariableInfo(src, window, round(coverage, 4), round(filled, 4))
    om_days = pd.date_range(*om_window).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    om_only = open_meteo.reindex(om_days)
    note = "station not usable for this variable" if not station_usable else \
        f"station coverage {coverage:.0%} < {min_coverage:.0%}; Open-Meteo used"
    return om_only, VariableInfo("open_meteo", om_window, round(float(om_only.notna().mean()), 4), 1.0, [note])


def rate_with_interval(k: int, n_days: int, level: float) -> dict:
    """Events per year from k events over n_days observed days, with an exact Poisson interval."""
    years = n_days / DAYS_PER_YEAR if n_days else 0.0
    if years == 0:
        return {"per_year": None, "lo": None, "hi": None, "events": k, "years": 0.0}
    a = 1 - level
    lo = 0.0 if k == 0 else chi2.ppf(a / 2, 2 * k) / 2
    hi = chi2.ppf(1 - a / 2, 2 * k + 2) / 2
    return {"per_year": k / years, "lo": lo / years, "hi": hi / years, "events": int(k), "years": round(years, 2)}


def disruption_flags(series: dict[str, pd.Series], wt: pd.DataFrame | None, tornado_dates: set[str],
                     th: dict) -> dict[str, pd.Series]:
    """Per-day boolean flags (NaN where the deciding variable is missing) for the station-based hazards."""
    snow, prcp, tmax, gust = (series[k] for k in ("snow_cm", "precip_mm", "tmax_c", "gust_kmh"))

    def flag(cond: pd.Series, base: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
        return cond.astype(float).where(base.notna())

    ice = pd.Series(0.0, index=snow.index)
    if wt is not None and not wt.empty:
        icy = wt.reindex(snow.index)[["wt_glaze", "wt_freezing_rain", "wt_ice_pellets"]].fillna(0).sum(axis=1) > 0
        ice = icy.astype(float)
    winter = flag((snow >= th["disruption_snow_cm"]) | (ice > 0), snow)

    torn = pd.Series(gust.index.isin(list(tornado_dates)), index=gust.index)
    convective = flag((gust >= th["disruption_gust_kmh"]) | torn, gust)
    return {
        "winter": winter,
        "flood": flag(prcp >= th["disruption_precip_mm"], prcp),
        "convective": convective,
        "heat": flag(tmax >= th["disruption_heat_c"], tmax),
    }


def descriptive_flags(series: dict[str, pd.Series], wt: pd.DataFrame | None, th: dict) -> dict[str, pd.Series]:
    """Per-day flags for metrics shown in answers (not used for ranking)."""
    snow, prcp, tmax, tmin, gust = (series[k] for k in ("snow_cm", "precip_mm", "tmax_c", "tmin_c", "gust_kmh"))

    def flag(cond, base):
        return cond.astype(float).where(base.notna())

    out = {
        "snow_day": flag(snow >= th["snow_day_cm"], snow),
        "trace_snow_day": flag(snow >= th["trace_snow_cm"], snow),
        "heavy_snow_day": flag(snow >= th["heavy_snow_cm"], snow),
        "extreme_cold_day": flag(tmin <= th["extreme_cold_c"], tmin),
        "heavy_rain_day": flag(prcp >= th["heavy_rain_mm"], prcp),
        "extreme_heat_day": flag(tmax >= th["extreme_heat_c"], tmax),
        "damaging_gust_day": flag(gust >= th["damaging_gust_kmh"], gust),
    }
    if wt is not None and not wt.empty:
        w = wt.reindex(snow.index).fillna(0)
        out["ice_day"] = ((w[["wt_glaze", "wt_freezing_rain", "wt_ice_pellets"]].sum(axis=1) > 0)).astype(float)
        out["thunder_day"] = (w["wt_thunder"] > 0).astype(float)
    return out


def summarize_flags(flags: pd.Series, level: float) -> dict:
    valid = flags.dropna()
    return rate_with_interval(int(valid.sum()), int(len(valid)), level)


def max_3day_precip_mean(prcp: pd.Series) -> float | None:
    """Average over years of each year's largest 3-day precipitation total (years with >= 80% data)."""
    s = prcp.copy()
    s.index = pd.to_datetime(s.index)
    roll = s.rolling(3, min_periods=3).sum()
    per_year = roll.groupby(roll.index.year).max()
    ok = s.notna().groupby(s.index.year).mean() >= 0.8
    vals = per_year[ok.reindex(per_year.index, fill_value=False)].dropna()
    return float(vals.mean()) if len(vals) else None


def warning_days(warnings: pd.DataFrame, tz: str, phenomena: dict[str, list[str]],
                 years: tuple[int, int]) -> dict[str, set[str]]:
    """Local calendar dates covered by at least one warning, per hazard.

    warnings: columns phenomena, issue, expire (UTC ISO strings). A warning covers every local
    date from its issue time to its expire time, inclusive.
    """
    out = {h: set() for h in phenomena}
    if warnings.empty:
        return out
    code_to_hazard = {c: h for h, codes in phenomena.items() for c in codes}
    w = warnings[warnings["phenomena"].isin(code_to_hazard)].copy()
    # The two IEM endpoints use slightly different ISO formats ("...T03:58Z" vs "...T03:58:00Z").
    def to_local_date(s):
        return pd.to_datetime(s, utc=True, format="ISO8601").dt.tz_convert(tz).dt.normalize().dt.tz_localize(None)

    w["start"], w["stop"] = to_local_date(w["issue"]), to_local_date(w["expire"])
    w["stop"] = w[["start", "stop"]].max(axis=1)
    lo, hi = str(years[0]), str(years[1])
    for code, s, e in zip(w["phenomena"], w["start"], w["stop"]):
        for d in pd.date_range(s, e).strftime("%Y-%m-%d"):
            if lo <= d[:4] <= hi:
                out[code_to_hazard[code]].add(d)
    return out


def dates_in_incidents(dates: set[str], incidents: pd.DataFrame) -> int:
    """How many dates fall inside any incident period (columns begin_date, end_date, ISO dates)."""
    if not dates or incidents.empty:
        return 0
    b, e = incidents["begin_date"].to_numpy(), incidents["end_date"].to_numpy()
    return sum(bool(((b <= d) & (e >= d)).any()) for d in dates)


def share_with_interval(k: int, n: int, level: float) -> dict:
    """Binomial share k/n with an exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval."""
    from scipy.stats import beta
    if n == 0:
        return {"share": 0.0, "lo": 0.0, "hi": 0.0, "k": 0, "n": 0}
    a = 1 - level
    lo = 0.0 if k == 0 else float(beta.ppf(a / 2, k, n - k + 1))
    hi = 1.0 if k == n else float(beta.ppf(1 - a / 2, k + 1, n - k))
    return {"share": k / n, "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "k": int(k), "n": int(n)}


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- database


def load_hub_daily(conn: sqlite3.Connection, hub_id: str) -> tuple[dict, dict, pd.DataFrame | None, dict]:
    """Return (series per variable, VariableInfo per variable, weather-type flags or None, station info)."""
    sp = get_params()["scoring"]
    window = (f"{sp['window'][0]}-01-01", f"{sp['window'][1]}-12-31")
    om_window = ("2016-01-01", f"{sp['window'][1]}-12-31")

    st_row = conn.execute("SELECT station_id, station_name, distance_km, gust_measured FROM hub_stations "
                          "WHERE hub_id = ?", (hub_id,)).fetchone()
    station = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM station_daily WHERE station_id = ?", conn,
                          params=(st_row[0],)).set_index("date") if st_row else pd.DataFrame()
    om = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM daily_weather WHERE hub_id = ?", conn, params=(hub_id,)).set_index("date")

    series, infos = {}, {}
    for var, (st_col, om_col) in VARIABLES.items():
        st_s = station[st_col] if st_col in station else pd.Series(dtype=float)
        usable = bool(st_row) and not (var == "gust_kmh" and not st_row[3])
        series[var], infos[var] = combine_variable(st_s, om[om_col], window, om_window, sp["min_coverage"], usable)

    # Weather-type flags are only trusted from full-instrument stations (gust_measured = 1).
    wt = station[WT_FLAGS] if (st_row and st_row[3] and not station.empty) else None
    st_info = {"station_id": st_row[0], "station_name": st_row[1], "distance_km": st_row[2],
               "gust_measured": bool(st_row[3])} if st_row else None
    return series, infos, wt, st_info

1	"""Scoring engine.
2	
3	KPIs (no chosen hazard weights):
4	- Routine disruption days/yr per hazard = days covered by an NWS warning for that hazard at the
5	  hub (county or forecast zone), 2006-2025. NWS criteria are set locally, so a warning means
6	  conditions expected to be dangerous *for that place*.
7	- Severity share per hazard = share of warning days (pooled over all hubs) that fall inside a
8	  FEMA major-disaster incident period of a matching type in the hub's county.
9	- Severe disruption days/yr = sum over hazards of routine days x severity share
10	  -> the primary ranking (resilience investment targets severe events).
11	Evidence kept for explanations: measured threshold days (station data 1996-2025), HURDAT2 storm
12	counts and named storms, SPC report days, descriptive climate metrics.
13	
14	Usage:
15	    python -m app.scoring.engine --print

43	    order = values.reset_index().sort_values([values.name, values.index.name], ascending=[False, True])
44	    labels = np.empty(len(order), dtype=object)

51	    reasons = []

143	    """Declarations matching a hazard by FEMA incident type OR by title (FEMA often files winter

    # A hub is linked to its NWS forecast zone and its county (hub_ugc). Zone and county products are counted

    # POINT:<hub_id> only when their polygon contains the hub, so a warning for the far side of a large county
    # is not counted.
    ugc = conn.execute("SELECT ugc, kind, timezone FROM hub_ugc WHERE hub_id=?", (hub_id,)).fetchall()

    for h in HAZARDS:
        # Warning days per year with an exact Poisson 90% range (rate of events over 20 years of days).
        r = m.rate_with_interval(len(wdays[h]), n_days, level)

def composite_days(hazard_days: dict[str, float], day_costs: dict[str, float] | None = None) -> float:
    """Total days per year across hazards, each hazard's days multiplied by its cost per day.

    Without analyst input every cost is 1 (default_day_costs in params.yaml), so the total is a plain sum and
    no hazard is weighted by our judgment. An analyst can pass day_costs (for example hurricane 3) to say that a
    hurricane day costs three times as much as an average day for their business.

def assign_tiers(values: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    """Label hubs High, Elevated or Low as the top, middle and bottom third of the network.

    Thirds are used because the measure has no external scale, so fixed cut-offs would be arbitrary. Hubs with
    equal values are ordered by hub id so the same data always gives the same tiers.
    """
    order = values.reset_index().sort_values([values.name, values.index.name], ascending=[False, True])
    labels = np.empty(len(order), dtype=object)
    # array_split handles network sizes that are not divisible by 3 (47 hubs gives groups of 16, 16 and 15).
    for label, idx in zip(("High", "Elevated", "Low"), np.array_split(np.arange(len(order)), 3)):
        labels[idx] = label
    return pd.Series(labels, index=order[values.index.name].to_numpy()).reindex(values.index)

"""Daily hub weather (station first, Open-Meteo as backup) and day-based metrics.

Pure functions (combine_variable, disruption_flags, rate_with_interval, descriptive flags)
take pandas objects and are unit-tested on synthetic data. load_hub_daily() wraps the

import sqlite3
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import chi2

from app.scoring.params import get_params

DAYS_PER_YEAR = 365.25

# variable -> (station_daily column, daily_weather (Open-Meteo) column)
VARIABLES = {
    "precip_mm": ("prcp_mm", "precip_mm"),
    "snow_cm": ("snow_cm", "snowfall_cm"),
    "tmax_c": ("tmax_c", "tmax_c"),
    "tmin_c": ("tmin_c", "tmin_c"),
    "gust_kmh": ("gust_kmh", "wind_gust_kmh"),
}
WT_FLAGS = ["wt_thunder", "wt_ice_pellets", "wt_hail", "wt_glaze", "wt_freezing_rain"]


@dataclass
class VariableInfo:
    source: str              # station | station+open_meteo | open_meteo
    window: tuple[str, str]  # dates actually used
    coverage: float          # share of window days with a value
    filled_share: float      # share of used values that came from Open-Meteo
    notes: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


def combine_variable(station: pd.Series, open_meteo: pd.Series, window: tuple[str, str],
                     om_window: tuple[str, str], min_coverage: float,
                     station_usable: bool = True) -> tuple[pd.Series, VariableInfo]:
    """Station value where present, else Open-Meteo. If coverage stays below min_coverage
    (or the station can't be used for this variable), use Open-Meteo alone over its window."""
    days = pd.date_range(*window).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    st = station.reindex(days) if station_usable else pd.Series(np.nan, index=days)
    om = open_meteo.reindex(days)
    combined = st.combine_first(om)
    coverage = float(combined.notna().mean())
    if station_usable and coverage >= min_coverage:
        filled = float((st.isna() & om.notna()).sum() / max(combined.notna().sum(), 1))
        src = "station" if filled == 0 else "station+open_meteo"
        return combined, VariableInfo(src, window, round(coverage, 4), round(filled, 4))
    om_days = pd.date_range(*om_window).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    om_only = open_meteo.reindex(om_days)
    note = "station not usable for this variable" if not station_usable else \
        f"station coverage {coverage:.0%} < {min_coverage:.0%}; Open-Meteo used"
    return om_only, VariableInfo("open_meteo", om_window, round(float(om_only.notna().mean()), 4), 1.0, [note])

    if years == 0:
