"""Deterministic cleanup of answer text.

Removes typographic habits that read as machine-written: em dashes, en dashes and the ellipsis character.
The prompt already asks the model to avoid them; this code makes the result independent of whether it did.
Numbers are never changed, so number tracing is unaffected.

The characters are written as escape codes (EM_DASH and so on) so this source file stays plain ASCII.
"""

import re

EM_DASH = "\u2014"
EN_DASH = "\u2013"
ELLIPSIS = "\u2026"

# A number range written with an en dash ("1.03" en dash "1.75") becomes "1.03 to 1.75".
_RANGE = re.compile(r"(\d)\s*" + EN_DASH + r"\s*(?=[-+]?\d)")
# An em dash between spaced words ("word" space em dash space "word") becomes a comma.
_EM_SPACED = re.compile(r"\s+" + EM_DASH + r"\s+")
# An em dash directly between two words becomes a comma as well.
_EM_TIGHT = re.compile(r"(?<=\w)" + EM_DASH + r"(?=\w)")


def clean_text(s: str) -> str:
    """Replace dashes and ellipsis characters in one string with plain punctuation."""
    if not s:
        return s
    s = _RANGE.sub(r"\1 to ", s)
    s = _EM_SPACED.sub(", ", s)
    s = _EM_TIGHT.sub(", ", s)
    # Any remaining cases: em dash to comma, en dash to hyphen, ellipsis character to three dots.
    s = s.replace(EM_DASH, ", ").replace(EN_DASH, "-").replace(ELLIPSIS, "...")
    return re.sub(r",\s*,", ",", s)   # collapse a double comma created by the replacements


def clean_answer(answer: dict) -> dict:
    """Clean every human-readable text field of a FinalAnswer dict."""
    a = dict(answer)
    a["answer_markdown"] = clean_text(a.get("answer_markdown", ""))
    a["assumptions"] = [clean_text(x) for x in a.get("assumptions", [])]
    a["suggested_followups"] = [clean_text(x) for x in a.get("suggested_followups", [])]
    if isinstance(a.get("uncertainty"), dict):
        a["uncertainty"] = {**a["uncertainty"], "reasons": [clean_text(x) for x in a["uncertainty"].get("reasons", [])]}
    for h in a.get("hubs", []):
        h["key_drivers"] = [clean_text(x) for x in h.get("key_drivers", [])]
    return a

Typographic characters are written as escape codes so this file stays plain ASCII.

from app.agent.textclean import ELLIPSIS, EM_DASH, EN_DASH, clean_answer, clean_text
from app.agent.validator import numbers_in_text


def test_dashes_and_ellipses_removed():
    assert clean_text(f"Heat adds nothing {EM_DASH} not because heat is harmless.") == \
        "Heat adds nothing, not because heat is harmless."
    assert clean_text(f"90% range: 1.03{EN_DASH}1.75 days") == "90% range: 1.03 to 1.75 days"
    assert clean_text(f"flooding{EM_DASH}then storms") == "flooding, then storms"
    assert clean_text(f"Working on it{ELLIPSIS}") == "Working on it..."
    assert clean_text(f"Dec 12 {EN_DASH} Mar 14") == "Dec 12 - Mar 14"


def test_numbers_are_unchanged():
    s = f"Dallas ranks 14 of 47 at 1.32 days/yr (90% range 1.03{EN_DASH}1.75) {EM_DASH} flood 0.88."
    assert [v for _, v, _, _ in numbers_in_text(clean_text(s))] == [v for _, v, _, _ in numbers_in_text(s)]


def test_clean_answer_fields():
    d = f" {EM_DASH} "
    a = clean_answer({"answer_markdown": f"a{d}b", "assumptions": [f"x{d}y"], "suggested_followups": [f"p{d}q"],
                      "uncertainty": {"level": "low", "reasons": [f"r{d}s"]}, "hubs": [{"key_drivers": [f"k{d}l"]}]})
    assert EM_DASH not in str(a)

Typographic characters are written as escape codes so this file stays plain ASCII.

from app.agent.textclean import ELLIPSIS, EM_DASH, EN_DASH, clean_answer, clean_text
from app.agent.validator import numbers_in_text


def test_dashes_and_ellipses_removed():
    assert clean_text(f"Heat adds nothing {EM_DASH} not because heat is harmless.") == \
        "Heat adds nothing, not because heat is harmless."
    assert clean_text(f"90% range: 1.03{EN_DASH}1.75 days") == "90% range: 1.03 to 1.75 days"
    assert clean_text(f"flooding{EM_DASH}then storms") == "flooding, then storms"
    assert clean_text(f"Working on it{ELLIPSIS}") == "Working on it..."
    assert clean_text(f"Dec 12 {EN_DASH} Mar 14") == "Dec 12 - Mar 14"


def test_numbers_are_unchanged():
    s = f"Dallas ranks 14 of 47 at 1.32 days/yr (90% range 1.03{EN_DASH}1.75) {EM_DASH} flood 0.88."
    assert [v for _, v, _, _ in numbers_in_text(clean_text(s))] == [v for _, v, _, _ in numbers_in_text(s)]


def test_clean_answer_fields():
    d = f" {EM_DASH} "
    a = clean_answer({"answer_markdown": f"a{d}b", "assumptions": [f"x{d}y"], "suggested_followups": [f"p{d}q"],
                      "uncertainty": {"level": "low", "reasons": [f"r{d}s"]}, "hubs": [{"key_drivers": [f"k{d}l"]}]})
    assert EM_DASH not in str(a)

from app.agent.textclean import clean_answer, clean_text
from app.agent.validator import numbers_in_text


def test_dashes_and_ellipses_removed():
    assert clean_text("Heat adds nothing — not because heat is harmless.") == \
        "Heat adds nothing, not because heat is harmless."
    assert clean_text("90% range: 1.03–1.75 days") == "90% range: 1.03 to 1.75 days"
    assert clean_text("flooding—then storms") == "flooding, then storms"
    assert clean_text("Working on it…") == "Working on it..."
    assert clean_text("Dec 12 – Mar 14") == "Dec 12 - Mar 14"


def test_numbers_are_unchanged():
    s = "Dallas ranks 14 of 47 at 1.32 days/yr (90% range 1.03–1.75) — flood 0.88."
    assert [v for _, v, _, _ in numbers_in_text(clean_text(s))] == [v for _, v, _, _ in numbers_in_text(s)]


def test_clean_answer_fields():
    a = clean_answer({"answer_markdown": "a — b", "assumptions": ["x — y"], "suggested_followups": ["p — q"],
                      "uncertainty": {"level": "low", "reasons": ["r — s"]}, "hubs": [{"key_drivers": ["k — l"]}]})
    assert "—" not in str(a)

"""Deterministic cleanup of answer text.

Removes typographic habits that read as machine-written: em dashes, en dashes and the ellipsis character.
The prompt already asks the model to avoid them; this code makes the result independent of whether it did.
Numbers are never changed, so number tracing is unaffected.

The characters are defined by their code points (EM_DASH and so on) so this source file stays plain ASCII.
"""

import re

EM_DASH = chr(0x2014)
EN_DASH = chr(0x2013)
ELLIPSIS = chr(0x2026)

# A number range written with an en dash ("1.03" en dash "1.75") becomes "1.03 to 1.75".
_RANGE = re.compile(r"(\d)\s*" + EN_DASH + r"\s*(?=[-+]?\d)")
# An em dash between spaced words ("word" space em dash space "word") becomes a comma.
_EM_SPACED = re.compile(r"\s+" + EM_DASH + r"\s+")

content.text:
The comment pass is done and the 125 tests pass. The review found one real data problem, which I measured but haven't changed. The comment changes are committed locally (4698e13) but not pushed.

## Comment pass

- **What I added:**
  - an explanation at the top of every module;
  - a description on every function;
  - comments on every step where the reason isn't obvious from the code, for example why scoring runs in two passes, or why model data is only used for the years it covers.
- **Plain ASCII:** every source file now contains only plain ASCII characters, checked by a script. Where code has to handle the dash characters (the text cleaner and its tests), they're defined by code number instead of typed.
- **Two small fixes found along the way:**
  - Nothing stopped an analyst's cost per day from being zero or negative, which would silently drop a hazard or flip the ranking. It's now rejected.
  - An unused library (`mcp`) is removed from the requirements.

## Review: are we broad but shallow?

No. The core is deep: the deterministic scoring, the strict contract between model and code, number tracing, 20 evaluation cases passing 40 of 40, and documented decisions. The extras (voice, seasonal outlook, stand-in hubs) are built, tested and reuse the same core. Adding alerts now would add breadth, not depth. The two items below matter more.

**1. Long-warning data problem (affects the ranking; needs your decision)**
- One Indianapolis flood warning in the archive runs 85 days (February to May 2009), and no FEMA disaster was declared there that year. It supplies up to 85 of Indianapolis's 188 flood warning days and lifts it to 4th place.
- A general rule fixes it: count at most N days per warning, where N is that warning type's 99th-percentile length across all hubs. That's 5 days for flood warnings and 9 for heat.
- I tested this on a copy of the database:
  - only 123 of 13,277 warnings are shortened;
  - the overall ranking barely changes (rank correlation 0.992);
  - Indianapolis moves from 4th to 14th;
  - Fargo moves from 5th to 10th.
- The honest trade-off: Fargo's 2011 Red River flood really did last weeks, so the cap undercounts some real long floods.
- I still recommend the cap. An 85-day warning isn't plausible, and a rule derived from the data, applied to every hub, is defensible in the interview. The trade-off goes into DECISIONS.md.
- Doing it means rescoring, updating the numbers quoted in the docs, and a short evaluation run (about 30 to 40 minutes).

**2. Lost conversations after a restart (affects users; about 15 minutes)**
Conversations are kept in the server's memory. On Render's free plan the service sleeps when idle, and every push redeploys it. After that, a follow-up like "what about Chicago?" silently loses its context. The fix is to have the server say when it started a fresh conversation, and show a one-line note in the chat.

**3. Known limits I'd document rather than fix**
- **Long FEMA incident periods:** some flood declarations cover up to 5 months, which may overstate the flood severity share. This is already listed as a limitation.
- **Rate limit can be bypassed:** it identifies users by a header that a client can fake. The real cost guard is the daily budget cap, so the risk is small.
- **Unrecorded cost of failed answers:** if the model fails partway through an answer, the cost of the calls already made isn't counted against the daily budget. This is minor.

**4. Leftovers for alerts:** an empty `app/alerts` package, an `ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` setting, an empty `alerts` table and the `APScheduler` library. I'd remove them if we skip alerts, so the repo has no dead code.

My recommendation: fix items 1 and 2, document item 3, remove the alert leftovers, skip alerts, then go to the final checks (Phase 13).

content.text:
## Is the cap overfitting?

It's valid outlier handling, as long as we follow a few rules.

Overfitting would mean choosing or adjusting a rule because it makes the results look the way we want, for example "Indianapolis looks too high, so let's change something until it drops." What separates this fix from that:

- **The trigger was a data-quality check, not a ranking we disliked.** A flood warning lasting 85 days isn't plausible for this warning type. Its 99th-percentile length is 5 days, so this record is about 17 times longer.
- **The rule is general.** It applies the same way to every warning type and every hub, and doesn't mention Indianapolis.
- **The threshold comes from the data's own distribution, not from the rankings.** Each type's 99th-percentile length is computed from all warnings. Capping extreme values at a high percentile is a standard robust-statistics method (called winsorizing).
- **It's mostly neutral.** Only 123 of 13,277 warnings change, and the overall ranking barely moves (rank correlation 0.992).

There's one honest weakness. We found the problem while looking at one hub, and we've already seen what the fix does to the ranking. To keep it clean:

1. **Pick the threshold once, on principle (the 99th percentile), and don't tune it.** No trying the 95th or 99.9th to see which ranking looks better.
2. **Document it with its cost.** It also shortens real long events, such as Fargo's 2011 Red River flood, which drops from 5th to 10th.
3. **Report both versions** in DECISIONS.md: the ranking with and without the cap, and the 0.992 correlation.

That's an answer you can defend in the interview: "I found an implausible record, fixed it with a general rule derived from the data, and here is exactly what it changed."

## Fix 2: a better option than a countdown

The 15 minutes is Render putting the service to sleep, and the app can't control or delay that. A "you'll lose context in X minutes" warning would also appear while the person is away, so they'd miss it anyway.

Simpler and better:

- **Keep the service awake while the page is open.** The page sends a tiny request to `/health` every 10 minutes. That doesn't use the AI model, so it costs nothing. While someone has the app open, the service never sleeps and the conversation is never lost.
- **Show a one-line note if a conversation is still lost** (after a redeploy, or when a tab is reopened later): "Your earlier conversation expired, so I started a new one. Please repeat any details I need."

Together that's still about 15 to 20 minutes. If you agree, I'll do the cap first (rescore, update the docs and numbers, short evaluation run), then fix 2, then remove the alert leftovers and push.

    # Main measure: days with an NWS warning at the hub.
    # A hub is linked to its NWS forecast zone and its county (hub_ugc). Zone and county products are counted
    # as issued. Storm-based warnings (thunderstorm, tornado, flash flood) were stored under the special code
    # POINT:<hub_id> only when their polygon contains the hub, so a warning for the far side of a large county
    # is not counted.
    ugc = conn.execute("SELECT ugc, kind, timezone FROM hub_ugc WHERE hub_id=?", (hub_id,)).fetchall()
    tz = ugc[0][2] if ugc else "UTC"   # local time zone, so a warning day is a local calendar day
    codes = [u[0] for u in ugc] + [f"POINT:{hub_id}"]
    warns = pd.read_sql(f"SELECT phenomena, issue, expire FROM nws_warnings WHERE ugc IN "

def test_warning_spanning_midnight_covers_both_local_dates():
    w = pd.DataFrame({"phenomena": ["WS"], "issue": ["2021-02-14T03:00:00Z"], "expire": ["2021-02-15T06:00:00Z"]})
    # 03:00Z = 21:00 previous day in Chicago (UTC-6)

    all_warnings = pd.read_sql("SELECT phenomena, issue, expire FROM nws_warnings", conn)

"""Seasonal (climatological) outlook per hub x hazard x calendar month.

For each month: in how many of the years 2006-2025 the hub had at least one NWS warning day for
the hazard (with an exact binomial range), the average number of warning days, and the expected
severe disruption days (average warning days x the hazard's FEMA severity share). Hurricanes also
get a long-record frequency from HURDAT2 storm days within 150 km, 1950-2025.

This is historical frequency ("how often it happened in this month"), not a forecast.

    python -m app.scoring.seasonal
"""

import json
import sqlite3
from collections import defaultdict

import pandas as pd

from app.db import create_schema, get_connection
from app.scoring import metrics as m
from app.scoring.engine import HAZARDS
from app.scoring.params import get_params


def hub_warning_dates(conn: sqlite3.Connection, hub_id: str) -> dict[str, set[str]]:
    """Local dates with a warning at the hub, per hazard (same selection as the scoring engine)."""
    wp = get_params()["warnings"]
    ugc = conn.execute("SELECT ugc, timezone FROM hub_ugc WHERE hub_id=?", (hub_id,)).fetchall()
    codes = [u[0] for u in ugc] + [f"POINT:{hub_id}"]

"""Seasonal (climatological) outlook per hub x hazard x calendar month.

For each month: in how many of the years 2006-2025 the hub had at least one NWS warning day for
the hazard (with an exact binomial range), the average number of warning days, and the expected
severe disruption days (average warning days x the hazard's FEMA severity share). Hurricanes also
get a long-record frequency from HURDAT2 storm days within 150 km, 1950-2025.

This is historical frequency ("how often it happened in this month"), not a forecast.

    python -m app.scoring.seasonal
"""

import json
import sqlite3
from collections import defaultdict

import pandas as pd

from app.db import create_schema, get_connection
from app.scoring import metrics as m
from app.scoring.engine import HAZARDS
from app.scoring.params import get_params


def hub_warning_dates(conn: sqlite3.Connection, hub_id: str) -> dict[str, set[str]]:
    """Local dates with a warning at the hub, per hazard (same selection as the scoring engine)."""
    wp = get_params()["warnings"]
    ugc = conn.execute("SELECT ugc, timezone FROM hub_ugc WHERE hub_id=?", (hub_id,)).fetchall()
    codes = [u[0] for u in ugc] + [f"POINT:{hub_id}"]
    w = pd.read_sql(f"SELECT phenomena, issue, expire FROM nws_warnings WHERE ugc IN ({','.join('?' * len(codes))})",
                    conn, params=codes)
    return m.warning_days(w, ugc[0][1] if ugc else "UTC", wp["phenomena"], (wp["first_year"], wp["last_year"]))


def monthly_rows(hub_id: str, dates: dict[str, set[str]], shares: dict[str, float],
                 storm_dates: list[str], years: tuple[int, int], storm_years: tuple[int, int],
                 level: float) -> list[tuple]:
    """Pure function: rows for hub_monthly from warning dates per hazard.

    For each hazard and month: k = number of years (out of n_years) with at least one warning day in that
    month, the share k / n_years with an exact range, the average warning days in that month, and expected
    disaster-level days (average warning days x severity share). Hurricanes also get the share of years since
    1950 with a storm nearby in that month, because 20 years is short for a rare hazard.
    """
    n_years = years[1] - years[0] + 1
    n_storm_years = storm_years[1] - storm_years[0] + 1
    storm_by_month = defaultdict(set)
    for d in storm_dates:   # dates are YYYY-MM-DD text: d[:4] is the year, d[5:7] the month
        if storm_years[0] <= int(d[:4]) <= storm_years[1]:
            storm_by_month[int(d[5:7])].add(d[:4])
    rows = []
    for hazard in HAZARDS:
        by_month_year = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))
        for d in dates.get(hazard, ()):
            by_month_year[int(d[5:7])][d[:4]] += 1
        for month in range(1, 13):
            k = len(by_month_year[month])
            total_days = sum(by_month_year[month].values())
            ci = m.share_with_interval(k, n_years, level)
            mean_days = total_days / n_years
            longrecord = len(storm_by_month[month]) / n_storm_years if hazard == "hurricane" else None
            rows.append((hub_id, hazard, month, n_years, k, ci["share"], ci["lo"], ci["hi"], mean_days,
                         mean_days * shares.get(hazard, 0.0), longrecord))
    return rows


MONTH_ABBR = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
MIN_DAYS_FOR_SEASON = 5          # fewer warning days than this in 20 years: too few to describe a season
SEASON_COVERAGE = 0.8            # the season window covers >= 80% of warning days


def season_profile(dates: set[str], n_years: int) -> dict | None:
    """When a hazard happens and what its events look like, from its warning dates (pure function).

    - window: the shortest run of consecutive months (wrapping Dec->Jan) holding >= 80% of warning days
    - typical range: 10th-90th percentile dates of warning days inside that window
    - events: runs of consecutive warning days
    """
    if len(dates) < MIN_DAYS_FOR_SEASON:
        return None
    ds = sorted(pd.to_datetime(list(dates)))
    counts = [0] * 12
    for d in ds:
        counts[d.month - 1] += 1
    total = len(ds)
    # Try windows of 1 month, then 2, and so on; the first length that reaches the coverage wins, and among
    # windows of that length the one holding the most warning days is chosen.
    best = None
    for length in range(1, 13):
        for start in range(12):
            s = sum(counts[(start + i) % 12] for i in range(length))
            if s >= SEASON_COVERAGE * total and (best is None or s > best[2]):
                best = (start, length, s)
        if best:
            break
    start, length, covered = best
    months = [(start + i) % 12 for i in range(length)]
    # Typical date range: count days from the window start, so a November to March window does not break at
    # New Year. Every date is moved to the same non-leap year (2001) so day numbers are comparable.
    start_doy = pd.Timestamp(2001, start + 1, 1).day_of_year
    offsets = sorted(((d.replace(year=2001) if not (d.month == 2 and d.day == 29) else d.replace(year=2001, day=28))
                      .day_of_year - start_doy) % 365 for d in ds if d.month - 1 in months)
    # 10th and 90th percentile dates: the central 80% of warning days, ignoring rare very early or late ones.
    lo = offsets[int(0.1 * (len(offsets) - 1))]
    hi = offsets[int(round(0.9 * (len(offsets) - 1)))]
    to_md = lambda off: (pd.Timestamp(2001, 1, 1) + pd.Timedelta(days=(start_doy - 1 + off) % 365)).strftime("%b %d")  # noqa: E731
    # Events: runs of consecutive warning days. A 3-day blizzard warning is one event lasting 3 days.
    events, run_start, prev = [], ds[0], ds[0]
    for d in ds[1:]:
        if (d - prev).days > 1:
            events.append((run_start, (prev - run_start).days + 1))
            run_start = d
        prev = d
    events.append((run_start, (prev - run_start).days + 1))
    lengths = sorted(n for _, n in events)
    longest = max(events, key=lambda e: (e[1], e[0]))
    return {
        "usual_months": f"{MONTH_ABBR[months[0]]}-{MONTH_ABBR[months[-1]]}" if length > 1 else MONTH_ABBR[months[0]],
        "share_of_warning_days_in_usual_months": round(covered / total, 2),
        "peak_month": MONTH_ABBR[max(range(12), key=lambda i: (counts[i], -i))],
        "typical_dates": f"{to_md(lo)} - {to_md(hi)}",
        "events_per_year": round(len(events) / n_years, 1),
        "typical_event_days": int(lengths[len(lengths) // 2]),
        "longest_event_days": int(longest[1]),
        "longest_event_start": longest[0].strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
        "warning_days_observed": total,
    }


def compute(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> dict:
    """Rebuild hub_monthly and hub_hazard_season. Runs after scoring, because it uses the severity shares."""
    p = get_params()
    wp, hp = p["warnings"], p["event_rates"]["hurricane"]
    radius = p["event_rates"]["default_radius_km"]["hurricane"]
    details = json.loads(conn.execute("SELECT details_json FROM risk_scores ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0])
    shares = {h: details["hazards"][h]["severity_share"]["share"] for h in HAZARDS}
    create_schema(conn)
    conn.execute("DELETE FROM hub_monthly")
    conn.execute("DELETE FROM hub_hazard_season")
    total = 0
    n_years = wp["last_year"] - wp["first_year"] + 1
    for (hub_id,) in conn.execute("SELECT id FROM hubs ORDER BY id").fetchall():
        dates = hub_warning_dates(conn, hub_id)
        conn.executemany("INSERT INTO hub_hazard_season VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                         [(hub_id, h, json.dumps(season_profile(dates.get(h, set()), n_years))) for h in HAZARDS])
        row = conn.execute("SELECT details_json FROM hub_event_rates WHERE hub_id=? AND hazard='hurricane_days' "
                           "AND radius_km=?", (hub_id, radius)).fetchone()
        storm_dates = json.loads(row[0]).get("dates", []) if row else []
        rows = monthly_rows(hub_id, dates, shares, storm_dates, (wp["first_year"], wp["last_year"]),
                            (hp["first_year"], hp["last_year"]), p["event_rates"]["confidence_level"])
        conn.executemany("INSERT INTO hub_monthly VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
        total += len(rows)
    conn.commit()
    return {"rows": total}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(compute(get_connection()))

"""API tests with FastAPI's TestClient and a scripted fake LLM (no OpenAI calls)."""

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from app.agent.agent import Agent
from app.agent.llm_client import LLMUnavailableError
from app.api.guards import DailyBudget, RateLimiter
from app.config import get_settings
from tests.test_agent import FakeLLM, answer, resp

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not get_settings().db_file.exists(), reason="database not built")
CODE = {"X-Access-Code": "test-code"}


@pytest.fixture
def make_client(monkeypatch):
    def _make(responses=(), agent=None, **env):
        monkeypatch.setenv("APP_ACCESS_CODE", "test-code")
        monkeypatch.setenv("ADMIN_TOKEN", "admin-token")
        for k, v in env.items():
            monkeypatch.setenv(k, str(v))
        get_settings.cache_clear()
        from app.api.main import app
        app.state.agent = agent or Agent(llm=FakeLLM(list(responses) or [resp(text=answer("ok"))] * 20))
        return TestClient(app)
    yield _make
    get_settings.cache_clear()


def test_access_code_required(make_client):
    with make_client() as c:
        assert c.get("/api/hubs").status_code == 401
        assert c.get("/api/hubs", headers={"X-Access-Code": "wrong"}).status_code == 401
        assert c.get("/api/hubs", headers=CODE).status_code == 200
        assert c.get("/health").status_code == 200          # open
        assert c.get("/").status_code == 200                # static page open


def test_chat_round_trip_and_session(make_client):
    with make_client([resp(text=answer("first")), resp(text=answer("second"))]) as c:
        r1 = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q1"}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert r1["answer"]["answer_markdown"] == "first" and r1["session_id"]
        r2 = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q2", "session_id": r1["session_id"]}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert r2["session_id"] == r1["session_id"] and r2["answer"]["answer_markdown"] == "second"
        assert c.post("/api/chat/reset", json={"session_id": r1["session_id"]}, headers=CODE).status_code == 200


def test_chat_input_validation(make_client):
    with make_client() as c:
        assert c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": ""}, headers=CODE).status_code == 422
        assert c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "x" * 2001}, headers=CODE).status_code == 422


def test_rate_limit(make_client):
    with make_client(CHAT_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN=2) as c:
        codes = [c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q"}, headers=CODE).status_code for _ in range(3)]
        assert codes == [200, 200, 429]

"""In-memory conversation sessions.

We keep the conversation ourselves (not the provider's stored conversations): provider-neutral,
testable, and we can trim it. Old tool outputs are trimmed from what is sent to the model;
the full outputs are kept separately so the validator can still trace numbers from earlier turns.
"""

import threading
import time
import uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

TTL_SECONDS = 2 * 60 * 60    # a conversation unused for 2 hours is forgotten
KEEP_FULL_TURNS = 3          # tool outputs of the last 3 turns are sent to the model in full
TRIMMED = '{"trimmed": "older tool output removed to save context; call the tool again if needed"}'


@dataclass
class Session:
    """One conversation."""
    id: str
    items: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)          # conversation sent to the model
    turn_starts: list[int] = field(default_factory=list)     # index in items where each turn starts
    tool_outputs: list[tuple[str, dict]] = field(default_factory=list)  # (tool, full output), for validation
    last_used: float = field(default_factory=time.time)

    def start_turn(self) -> None:
        """Mark where a new turn begins, so trim() knows which outputs are old."""
        self.turn_starts.append(len(self.items))
        self.last_used = time.time()

    def trim(self, keep_turns: int = KEEP_FULL_TURNS) -> None:
        """Replace tool outputs older than the last `keep_turns` turns (calls stay paired with outputs)."""
        if len(self.turn_starts) <= keep_turns:
            return
        cutoff = self.turn_starts[-keep_turns]
        for item in self.items[:cutoff]:
            if item.get("type") == "function_call_output":
                item["output"] = TRIMMED


class SessionStore:
    """All conversations of this server process. Memory only: a restart starts every conversation fresh.

    A lock protects the dictionary because the API serves requests on several threads.
    """

    def __init__(self, ttl: int = TTL_SECONDS):
        self.ttl = ttl
        self._sessions: dict[str, Session] = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def get_or_create(self, session_id: str | None) -> Session:
        """Return the conversation with this id, or start a new one (also when the id has expired)."""
        with self._lock:
            self._expire()
            if session_id and session_id in self._sessions:
                return self._sessions[session_id]
            s = Session(id=session_id or uuid.uuid4().hex[:12])
            self._sessions[s.id] = s
            return s

    def reset(self, session_id: str) -> None:
        """Forget a conversation (the New chat button)."""
        with self._lock:
            self._sessions.pop(session_id, None)

    def _expire(self) -> None:
        """Drop conversations unused for longer than the time limit."""
        now = time.time()
        for sid in [k for k, s in self._sessions.items() if now - s.last_used > self.ttl]:
            del self._sessions[sid]

content.content:
## D5. Rules to keep the method honest

- **No parameter tuned to a ranking.** Every threshold, radius and pattern is in `app/scoring/params.yaml` with its reason. When a value needed a test, the test was decided before looking at the ranking it would produce. For example, the 150 km hurricane radius and 50 km storm radius were accepted because rankings stayed stable across nearby radii (rank correlation 0.83 to 0.98).
- **No hub-specific fixes.** When a single hub looked wrong, we looked for the general cause. Two examples:
  - Phoenix had 758 flash-flood warnings because Maricopa County is huge. The general fix: storm-based warnings count only when the warning polygon contains the hub. Phoenix dropped to 31, and every other large county was corrected the same way.
  - Some winter disasters were missing because FEMA filed them as "Severe Storm". The general fix: match declarations by type or by title keywords, with snowmelt and ice jams excluded from winter because they are floods.
- **No use of our own prior knowledge as data.** Expected answers in the evaluation are computed by calling the tools, never typed in by hand.

## D6. Tiers and uncertainty

**Tiers:** thirds of the network (High, Elevated, Low). Fixed cut-offs (for example "over 1 day is high") would be arbitrary because the measure is new and has no external scale. Thirds are simple to explain and always relative to the client's own network.

177:Two data problems found along the way were fixed in general ways:
178-
179:- **Large counties.** Counting every flash flood or thunderstorm warning that touched Maricopa County gave Phoenix 758 flash-flood warnings; counting only warning polygons that contain the hub gives 31. Storm-based warnings are now counted only when the polygon contains the hub.
180:- **Misfiled disasters.** FEMA often files winter disasters as "Severe Storm" or "Flood" (for example "SEVERE WINTER STORMS AND BLIZZARD CONDITIONS"). Declarations now match a hazard by type or by title keywords; snowmelt and ice-jam titles are excluded from winter because they are floods.
181-
182-### 5.3 Supporting calculations
183-
253:- **Warnings are forecasts.** NWS warnings include some false alarms and misses, and their criteria and names changed over time (for example "Excessive Heat" became "Extreme Heat" in 2024; both are counted).

lines: - *Choice:* cap each warning at the 99th-percentile duration of its type, computed from all stored warnings (`warnings.max_duration_percentile` in params.yaml). Deleting one record would be a hub-specific fix, and a fixed day limit would be our judgment; a percentile of the type's own distribution is derived from the data and treats every hub the same way.

- *Guarding against overfitting:* the problem was found while looking at one hub, and the effect on the ranking was measured before deciding. To keep the decision honest, the percentile was set once as standard outlier trimming (99th) and not tuned (no trying other percentiles to see which ranking looks better), and both rankings are reported here.

- *Effect:* 123 of 13,277 warnings are shortened. Rank correlation between the old and new ranking is 0.992; the top 3 are unchanged. Indianapolis moves from 4th to 14th (2.06 to 1.36 disaster-level days per year) and Fargo from 5th to 10th (1.91 to 1.58).

-  - *Cost:* genuinely long events are shortened too. The 2011 Red River flood at Fargo lasted weeks, and Fargo's flood warning days drop accordingly. We accept this because a month-long warning mostly repeats the same event, while a few unrealistic records would otherwise decide rankings.

+  - *Cost:* genuinely long events are shortened too. The 2011 Red River flood at Fargo lasted weeks, and Fargo's flood warning days drop accordingly. We accept this because the measure is meant to show how often a hazard strikes: a long event still counts, for up to its type's 99th-percentile length, while without the cap a handful of records, some of them likely errors, would decide rankings.
- **No use of our own prior knowledge as data.** Expected answers in the evaluation are computed by calling the tools, never typed in by hand.

- *Reading answers aloud*: a "Read aloud" switch reads each new answer, and a speaker button on every answer reads that one. The spoken text is built from the displayed answer: one sentence per paragraph, list item and table row, without markdown symbols, and "/yr" is read as "per year". It is spoken a few sentences at a time because Chrome stops long utterances after about 15 seconds. Reading stops when a new question is asked or a new chat starts.
- *Privacy*: in Chrome, speech recognition sends the audio to Google's speech service. A production deployment that must keep audio in-house would use a self-hosted speech model instead.

+**Conversation memory**: conversations are kept in the server's memory for 2 hours, which keeps the service simple and stateless on disk. On the free hosting plan the server sleeps after about 15 minutes without requests and loses that memory, as it does on every redeploy. Two measures handle this: while the page is open it checks `/health` every 10 minutes, which keeps the server awake at no model cost; and when the server receives a conversation id it no longer holds, the answer is shown with a note that the earlier conversation expired, so a follow-up question is never answered silently without its context. A production version would keep conversations in a shared store such as Redis or Postgres.

**Client view and developer view**: by default the interface shows what a client needs (the answer, a confidence badge, "Sources and reliability" with a confirmation that all figures were checked against the data, plain-language evidence in the hub panel). Tool calls, field-level number tracing, tokens and cost are available in a developer view (Methodology, "Show technical details", or `?dev=1`) for demonstrations.

Both fixes are done and live on https://weather-risk-agent-gz90.onrender.com. Its health check shows the new scoring version, and chat still requires the access code (pushed in 52d37c3). All 128 tests pass, and 20 of 20 evaluation cases pass against the real model.

**Fix 1: cap on long warnings**
- **How it works:** each warning now counts for at most the 99th-percentile duration of its own type, computed from all stored warnings. For example, that's 5 days for areal flood warnings and 9 for heat warnings. The percentile is a single documented setting (`max_duration_percentile: 99`), and I didn't try other values.
- **Tidier code:** scoring, the seasonal outlook and the weather-statistics tool used to each load a hub's warnings in their own copy of the code. They now share one function, so the cap applies the same way everywhere.
- **Effect on the scores:**
  - only 123 of 13,277 warnings were shortened;
  - the top 3 are unchanged, and the ranking correlates 0.992 with the old one;
  - Indianapolis moves from 4th to 14th, and Fargo from 5th to 10th.
- **Documentation:** DECISIONS.md records the options considered, why the threshold was chosen without tuning, the cost (Fargo's real 2011 flood is shortened too), and both rankings.
- **Tests:** two new unit tests cover the cap.

**Fix 2: lost conversations**
- **Keep-alive:** while the page is open, it checks the server's health every 10 minutes. That keeps the free-plan server from sleeping and doesn't use the AI model.
- **Expired note:** if a conversation is lost anyway (for example after a redeploy), the answer appears with the note "Your earlier conversation expired, so this answer starts a new one". I checked it in the browser, and a new API test covers it.

**Evaluation:**
- **One check fixed:** the first run passed 19 of 20, and the failure was in our check, not the answer. In the Miami vs Houston comparison, the model wrote "about once every 1.1 years" as the system prompt asks, but the check only accepted "0.93 days per year". The check now accepts either form, since both come from the same tool output.
- **Result:** that case then passed 3 of 3, and a fresh full run passed 20 of 20, at about 11 seconds and $0.013 per answer.
- **Documentation:** DESIGN.md records that finding.

All new code follows the standard you set: commented, plain ASCII. I saved that rule as a memory so it carries forward.

The alert leftovers are still in the repo for now: the empty `app/alerts` package, the `ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` setting, the `alerts` table and the APScheduler library. Whether they get used or removed depends on the alerts decision.

content.text:
## Alerts: what they need, what they add, what they risk

**What the assignment asks:** "a scheduled or webhook alert when a hub's risk score changes" (a bonus).

**Why the literal version has little value:** our scores are 20-year averages. They only change when the data is rebuilt, so a "score changed" alert would almost never fire. We could build it, but it would mostly demonstrate the plumbing.

**The meaningful version: live warning alerts.** Every 15 minutes, check the National Weather Service for active warnings at each hub (the same warning types our scoring uses). When a hub gets a new warning, or one ends, record an alert and post it to a webhook (Slack or a test URL). For example: "Jacksonville: Flood Warning issued, valid until 18:00." That answers the operational question "which hubs are disrupted right now", next to our historical "which hubs are exposed over time". It also shows integration work (scheduling, webhooks, external APIs), which is the core of an FDE role.

**What it requires (about 1.5 to 2 hours, done properly):**
1. **A small, separate module** (`app/alerts/monitor.py`) that:
   - fetches active warnings per hub;
   - compares them with the previous check;
   - stores new alerts in the existing `alerts` table;
   - sends the webhook if one is configured.
2. **An admin endpoint** that runs a check, plus `GET /api/alerts` to list recent alerts.
3. **Scheduling with a GitHub Actions cron job** that calls that endpoint every 15 minutes. A timer inside the server wouldn't work, because Render's free plan puts the server to sleep. Calling it from GitHub Actions also keeps the server awake.
4. **Unit tests** with recorded NWS responses (no network), plus a section in DESIGN.md and DECISIONS.md.
5. **Optional:** a small "active warning" badge on hubs in the leaderboard. I'd skip it to stay narrow.

**Risks to what we've built:**
- **Code risk: low if built as planned.** It doesn't touch scoring, the agent or the existing endpoints. It's a new module with its own tests, switched off unless configured.
- **Real risks:**
  - It's new code written under time pressure the night before submission.
  - It adds a runtime dependency on api.weather.gov. If that service is down, only the alerts fail, but it's another moving part to explain.
  - Alerts are stored in SQLite on Render's temporary disk, so they're lost on every redeploy. That's acceptable for a demo but must be documented.
  - It makes the AI session transcript longer.
- **Scope risk:** this is exactly the "broad versus deep" trade-off you raised. The core is complete and verified. Alerts would add one more feature, not more depth.

**My recommendation:** build it only if you have at least 2 hours left tonight and feel fresh. Otherwise skip it. In that case I remove the unused leftovers, and you point to the existing design in DESIGN.md section 11 ("designed, not built, and here is why live warnings beat score-change alerts"). A reviewer will value a clearly reasoned "not built" more than a rushed feature.

## What's left before submission (either way)

1. **Alerts decision:** build them, or remove the leftovers (`app/alerts`, the `ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` setting, the `alerts` table, APScheduler).
2. **PLAN.md header note.** It's the original plan and still mentions things we changed later (Claude Sonnet, hand-picked weights). Reviewers could take it as the final design. A two-line note at the top fixes that: "historical plan; the final design is in DESIGN.md and DECISIONS.md".
3. **Fresh-clone test:**
   - clone the repo into an empty folder;
   - install from scratch;
   - run the tests;
   - start the app.

   That proves the README instructions work for a reviewer.
4. **Secrets check:**
   - scan the repo and its whole git history for keys or codes;
   - confirm `.env` was never committed (already true);
   - confirm the access code isn't anywhere in the repo.
5. **Final live check by you:** the access code, one chat answer, the mic, and Read aloud on the Render URL.
6. **Export the AI session transcript** to `docs/ai-session/` (mandatory). This is last, after all changes, so it's complete.
7. **Final commit and push**, then look at the repo on GitHub as a reviewer would.
8. **Your submission message:** the live URL, the access code, the repo link, and a note that the free plan may take about a minute to wake up.

Without alerts this is about 45 to 60 minutes. With alerts, add 1.5 to 2 hours.

How much time do you have tonight? That decides the alerts question.

input.content:
"""Live warning monitor: alerts when a hub's current weather risk changes.

The risk scores describe 20 years of history and change only when the data is rebuilt, so alerting on score
changes would almost never fire. What changes day to day is whether a hub is under an active National Weather
Service warning right now. This module checks every hub against the NWS active-alerts API, compares the result
with the previous check, records each warning that starts or ends at a hub, and posts a summary to a webhook.

Rules that keep the alerts trustworthy:
- Only real warnings are tracked: status "Actual", VTEC significance W, and only the warning types our scoring
  counts (params.yaml, warnings.phenomena). Watches, advisories and statements are ignored.
- Each hub is queried by its point, so a warning counts only when its area contains the hub, the same idea as
  the storm-polygon rule in scoring.
- A warning is identified by its VTEC event id (office.type.W.number). The id stays the same when NWS updates
  or extends a warning, so an update is not reported as a new warning.
- If the request for a hub fails, that hub's state is left unchanged, so an API error never looks like
  "all warnings ended".
- The first check on a database where the monitor has never run is a baseline: warnings already active are
  recorded as "active_at_start" instead of "issued", so a fresh start or redeploy does not announce them as new.

Run one check from the command line:  python -m app.alerts.monitor
In production a scheduler calls POST /api/admin/alerts/check every 15 minutes (.github/workflows/alerts.yml).
"""

import json
import logging
import re
import sqlite3
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from typing import Callable

import httpx

from app.config import get_settings
from app.db import create_schema, get_connection
from app.ingest.common import USER_AGENT, now_iso
from app.scoring.params import get_params

log = logging.getLogger("alerts")

ACTIVE_ALERTS_URL = "https://api.weather.gov/alerts/active"
FETCH_WORKERS = 8         # parallel requests: 47 hubs take a few seconds without overloading the API
FETCH_TIMEOUT_S = 15

# A VTEC code describes one warning event, for example /O.EXT.KJAX.CF.W.0004.000000T0000Z-261126T0000Z/:
# product class O (operational, not a test), action EXT (extended), issuing office KJAX, warning type CF
# (coastal flood), significance W (warning) and event number 0004, followed by the valid time range.
VTEC_RE = re.compile(r"/O\.(?P<action>[A-Z]{3})\.(?P<office>[A-Z]{4})\.(?P<phen>[A-Z]{2})\.(?P<sig>[A-Z])\."
                     r"(?P<etn>\d{4})\.")
# Actions that announce the end of a warning; such a message means the warning is no longer active.
ENDED_ACTIONS = {"CAN", "EXP"}

# Only one check may run at a time (the scheduler and a manual call could overlap).
_RUN_LOCK = threading.Lock()


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ActiveWarning:
    """One NWS warning active at a hub."""
    event_key: str        # stable id, e.g. KJAX.CF.W.0004
    hazard: str           # our hazard group
    event: str            # NWS name, e.g. "Coastal Flood Warning"
    headline: str | None
    ends: str | None      # ISO time with the issuing office's UTC offset


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- pure functions


def warning_types() -> dict[str, str]:
    """NWS warning type code to our hazard group, from params.yaml (the same mapping scoring uses)."""
    return {code: hazard for hazard, codes in get_params()["warnings"]["phenomena"].items() for code in codes}


def parse_active(features: list[dict], types: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, ActiveWarning]:
    """Keep the real, still-active warnings of tracked types from an NWS alerts response (GeoJSON features)."""
    out: dict[str, ActiveWarning] = {}
    for feature in features:
        p = feature.get("properties") or {}
        if p.get("status") != "Actual":            # skip exercises, tests and drafts
            continue
        for vtec in (p.get("parameters") or {}).get("VTEC") or []:
            m = VTEC_RE.search(vtec)
            if not m or m["sig"] != "W" or m["phen"] not in types or m["action"] in ENDED_ACTIONS:
                continue
            key = f"{m['office']}.{m['phen']}.W.{m['etn']}"
            out[key] = ActiveWarning(key, types[m["phen"]], p.get("event") or m["phen"], p.get("headline"),
                                     p.get("ends") or p.get("expires"))
    return out


def summary_text(alerts: list[dict], checked_at: str) -> str:
    """Plain-text webhook message listing the alerts of one check (readable in Slack or any webhook viewer)."""
    verbs = {"issued": "issued", "ended": "ended", "active_at_start": "active when monitoring started"}
    lines = [f"Hub weather alerts (check at {checked_at[:16].replace('T', ' ')} UTC)"]
    for a in alerts:
        until = f", until {a['ends'][:16].replace('T', ' ')} local time" if a["kind"] != "ended" and a["ends"] else ""
        lines.append(f"- {a['hub_name']}, {a['state']}: {a['event']} {verbs[a['kind']]}{until}")
    return "\n".join(lines)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- network


def fetch_active(lat: float, lon: float) -> list[dict]:
    """Active NWS alerts whose area contains the point. Raises on network or HTTP errors."""
    with httpx.Client(timeout=FETCH_TIMEOUT_S, headers={"User-Agent": USER_AGENT,
                                                        "Accept": "application/geo+json"}) as client:

  counts (params.yaml, warnings.phenomena). Watches, advisories and statements are ignored.
- Each hub is queried by its point, so a warning counts only when its area contains the hub, the same idea as
  the storm-polygon rule in scoring.
- A warning is identified by its VTEC event id (office.type.W.number). The id stays the same when NWS updates
  or extends a warning, so an update is not reported as a new warning.
- If the request for a hub fails, that hub's state is left unchanged, so an API error never looks like
  "all warnings ended".

  recorded as "active_at_start" instead of "issued", so a fresh start or redeploy does not announce them as new.

# Live warning alerts: every 15 minutes, ask the deployed app to check all hubs for NWS warnings that started
# or ended (app/alerts/monitor.py). The scheduler lives here rather than inside the server because the free
# hosting plan puts the server to sleep when idle; a request from here wakes it.
#
# Setup (GitHub repository: Settings, then Secrets and variables, then Actions):
#   Secret   ADMIN_TOKEN = the ADMIN_TOKEN configured on Render
#   Variable APP_URL     = the deployed URL, for example https://weather-risk-agent-gz90.onrender.com
# Without both values the job does nothing.

name: Hub alert check

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "*/15 * * * *"     # every 15 minutes; GitHub may start scheduled runs a few minutes late
  workflow_dispatch: {}         # adds a "Run workflow" button for a manual check

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - name: Run one alert check
        env:
          APP_URL: ${{ vars.APP_URL }}
          ADMIN_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ADMIN_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "$APP_URL" ] || [ -z "$ADMIN_TOKEN" ]; then
            echo "APP_URL or ADMIN_TOKEN is not configured; skipping."
            exit 0
          fi
          # A sleeping server can take about a minute to wake up, hence the long timeout and the retries.
          curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error --max-time 180 --retry 2 --retry-delay 20 \
            -X POST -H "X-Admin-Token: $ADMIN_TOKEN" "$APP_URL/api/admin/alerts/check"

"""Tests for the live warning monitor, with recorded-style NWS responses (no network, temporary database)."""

import pytest

from app.alerts import monitor
from app.db import create_schema, get_connection

# Two test hubs; the fake fetch below answers by latitude.
HUBS = [("alpha", "Alpha", "FL", 30.0, -81.0), ("beta", "Beta", "TX", 29.0, -95.0)]


def feature(vtec: str, event: str = "Flood Warning", status: str = "Actual", ends: str = "2026-11-25T19:00:00-05:00"):
    """One alert in the shape the NWS API returns (only the fields the monitor reads)."""
    return {"properties": {"status": status, "event": event, "headline": f"{event} for the area",
                           "ends": ends, "expires": ends, "parameters": {"VTEC": [vtec]}}}


FLOOD_NEW = "/O.NEW.KJAX.FA.W.0001.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/"
FLOOD_EXT = "/O.EXT.KJAX.FA.W.0001.000000T0000Z-261125T0000Z/"   # same event, extended
WINTER_NEW = "/O.NEW.KHGX.WS.W.0007.261123T1800Z-261124T1200Z/"


@pytest.fixture
def conn(tmp_path):
    c = get_connection(tmp_path / "alerts.db")
    create_schema(c)
    c.executemany("INSERT INTO hubs (id, name, state, region, lat, lon, county_fips) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'South', ?, ?, '00000')",
                  HUBS)
    c.commit()
    yield c
    c.close()


def fetcher(responses: dict):
    """Fake fetch: responses maps hub latitude to a feature list, or to an exception to raise."""
    def fetch(lat, lon):
        r = responses.get(lat, [])
        if isinstance(r, Exception):
            raise r
        return r
    return fetch


class Recorder:
    """Fake webhook that records what was posted, or fails when asked to."""

    def __init__(self, fail: Exception | None = None):
        self.payloads, self.fail = [], fail

    def __call__(self, url, payload):
        if self.fail:
            raise self.fail
        self.payloads.append(payload)


def check(conn, responses, post=None, url="https://example.test/hook", t="2026-11-23T18:00:00+00:00"):
    return monitor.run_check(conn, fetch=fetcher(responses), post=post or Recorder(), webhook_url=url, checked_at=t)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- parsing


def test_parse_keeps_only_real_active_warnings_of_tracked_types():
    types = monitor.warning_types()
    features = [
        feature(FLOOD_NEW),                                                    # kept
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.FA.A.0002.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", "Flood Watch"),       # watch: ignored
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.CF.Y.0003.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", "Coastal Flood Advisory"),  # advisory
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.FL.W.0004.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", "Flood Warning"),     # river gauge: not tracked
        feature("/T.NEW.KJAX.FA.W.0005.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/"),           # test product class: ignored
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.FA.W.0006.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", status="Exercise"),    # exercise: ignored
        feature("/O.CAN.KJAX.FA.W.0008.000000T0000Z-261124T0000Z/"),           # cancelled: no longer active
    ]
    active = monitor.parse_active(features, types)
    assert list(active) == ["KJAX.FA.W.0001"] and active["KJAX.FA.W.0001"].hazard == "flood"


def test_an_extension_keeps_the_same_event_key():
    types = monitor.warning_types()
    assert monitor.parse_active([feature(FLOOD_NEW)], types).keys() == \
        monitor.parse_active([feature(FLOOD_EXT)], types).keys()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- checks over time


def test_first_check_is_a_baseline_not_new_alerts(conn):
    hook = Recorder()
    s = check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, post=hook)
    assert s["baseline"] and s["active_at_start"] == 1 and s["issued"] == 0 and s["active_now"] == 1
    assert "active when monitoring started" in hook.payloads[0]["text"]


def test_new_warning_is_issued_then_ended(conn):
    check(conn, {})                                                     # baseline with nothing active
    hook = Recorder()
    s = check(conn, {29.0: [feature(WINTER_NEW, "Winter Storm Warning")]}, post=hook, t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    assert (s["issued"], s["ended"], s["active_now"], s["webhook"]) == (1, 0, 1, "sent")
    assert "Beta, TX: Winter Storm Warning issued" in hook.payloads[0]["text"]
    s = check(conn, {}, t="2026-11-23T18:30:00+00:00")                 # no longer listed by NWS
    assert (s["issued"], s["ended"], s["active_now"]) == (0, 1, 0)


def test_update_of_the_same_warning_is_not_a_new_alert(conn):
    check(conn, {})
    check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    s = check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_EXT, ends="2026-11-26T07:00:00-05:00")]}, t="2026-11-23T18:30:00+00:00")
    assert (s["issued"], s["ended"], s["active_now"]) == (0, 0, 1)
    assert conn.execute("SELECT ends FROM active_warnings").fetchone()[0] == "2026-11-26T07:00:00-05:00"


def test_failed_request_leaves_the_hub_unchanged(conn):
    check(conn, {})
    check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    s = check(conn, {30.0: RuntimeError("NWS API unavailable")}, t="2026-11-23T18:30:00+00:00")
    assert s["hubs_failed"] == ["alpha"] and s["ended"] == 0 and s["active_now"] == 1


def test_webhook_failure_is_recorded_without_the_url(conn):
    class HTTPStatusError(Exception):
        response = type("R", (), {"status_code": 404})()

    check(conn, {})
    s = check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, post=Recorder(fail=HTTPStatusError("404 for url https://secret.test/x")),
              t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    assert s["webhook"] == "failed: HTTPStatusError (HTTP 404)" and "secret" not in s["webhook"]
    delivered, error = conn.execute("SELECT delivered, delivery_error FROM hub_alerts").fetchone()
    assert delivered == 0 and "secret" not in error


def test_without_a_webhook_alerts_are_still_recorded(conn):
    check(conn, {}, url=None)
    s = check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, url=None, t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    assert s["webhook"] == "not configured" and s["issued"] == 1
    r = monitor.recent(conn)
    assert r["active_warnings"][0]["hub_id"] == "alpha" and r["recent_alerts"][0]["kind"] == "issued"
    assert r["last_check"]["checked_at"] == "2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00"

"""API tests with FastAPI's TestClient and a scripted fake LLM (no OpenAI calls)."""

import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from app.agent.agent import Agent
from app.agent.llm_client import LLMUnavailableError
from app.api.guards import DailyBudget, RateLimiter
from app.config import get_settings
from tests.test_agent import FakeLLM, answer, resp

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not get_settings().db_file.exists(), reason="database not built")
CODE = {"X-Access-Code": "test-code"}


@pytest.fixture
def make_client(monkeypatch):
    def _make(responses=(), agent=None, **env):
        monkeypatch.setenv("APP_ACCESS_CODE", "test-code")
        monkeypatch.setenv("ADMIN_TOKEN", "admin-token")
        for k, v in env.items():
            monkeypatch.setenv(k, str(v))
        get_settings.cache_clear()
        from app.api.main import app
        app.state.agent = agent or Agent(llm=FakeLLM(list(responses) or [resp(text=answer("ok"))] * 20))
        return TestClient(app)
    yield _make
    get_settings.cache_clear()


def test_access_code_required(make_client):
    with make_client() as c:
        assert c.get("/api/hubs").status_code == 401
        assert c.get("/api/hubs", headers={"X-Access-Code": "wrong"}).status_code == 401
        assert c.get("/api/hubs", headers=CODE).status_code == 200
        assert c.get("/health").status_code == 200          # open
        assert c.get("/").status_code == 200                # static page open


def test_chat_round_trip_and_session(make_client):
    with make_client([resp(text=answer("first")), resp(text=answer("second"))]) as c:
        r1 = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q1"}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert r1["answer"]["answer_markdown"] == "first" and r1["session_id"]
        r2 = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q2", "session_id": r1["session_id"]}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert r2["session_id"] == r1["session_id"] and r2["answer"]["answer_markdown"] == "second"
        assert c.post("/api/chat/reset", json={"session_id": r1["session_id"]}, headers=CODE).status_code == 200


def test_unknown_session_is_reported_as_expired(make_client):
    # A conversation id the server does not hold (expired, or lost in a restart) starts fresh and is flagged;
    # the next turn in that new conversation is not flagged.
    with make_client([resp(text=answer("a")), resp(text=answer("b")), resp(text=answer("c"))]) as c:
        assert c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q"}, headers=CODE).json()["session_expired"] is False
        r = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q", "session_id": "lost123"}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert r["session_expired"] is True and r["session_id"] == "lost123"
        r2 = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q", "session_id": "lost123"}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert r2["session_expired"] is False


def test_chat_input_validation(make_client):
    with make_client() as c:
        assert c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": ""}, headers=CODE).status_code == 422
        assert c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "x" * 2001}, headers=CODE).status_code == 422


def test_rate_limit(make_client):
    with make_client(CHAT_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN=2) as c:
        codes = [c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q"}, headers=CODE).status_code for _ in range(3)]
        assert codes == [200, 200, 429]


def test_daily_budget_blocks_chat_but_not_data(make_client):
    with make_client(DAILY_BUDGET_USD=0.0015) as c:        # fake responses cost $0.001 each
        assert c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q"}, headers=CODE).status_code == 200
        assert c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q"}, headers=CODE).status_code == 200
        r = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q"}, headers=CODE)
        assert r.status_code == 429 and "budget" in r.json()["detail"]
        assert c.get("/api/scores", headers=CODE).status_code == 200
        assert c.get("/health").json()["budget"]["remaining_usd"] == 0


def test_admin_can_raise_budget(make_client):
    with make_client(DAILY_BUDGET_USD=1) as c:
        assert c.post("/api/admin/budget", json={"daily_budget_usd": 5}).status_code == 401
        r = c.post("/api/admin/budget", json={"daily_budget_usd": 5}, headers={"X-Admin-Token": "admin-token"})
        assert r.status_code == 200 and r.json()["cap_usd"] == 5


def test_llm_outage_returns_502(make_client):
    class Down:
        store = None

        def run_turn(self, *a, **k):
            raise LLMUnavailableError("down")
    with make_client(agent=Down()) as c:
        r = c.post("/api/chat", json={"message": "q"}, headers=CODE)
        assert r.status_code == 502 and "temporarily unavailable" in r.json()["detail"]


def test_data_endpoints(make_client):
    with make_client() as c:
        s = c.get("/api/scores", params={"hazard": "winter", "region": "Midwest", "top_n": 3}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert len(s["ranking"]) == 3 and all(r["region"] == "Midwest" for r in s["ranking"])
        assert c.get("/api/scores", params={"region": "Mars"}, headers=CODE).status_code == 422
        assert c.get("/api/hubs/dallas/breakdown", headers=CODE).json()["hub_id"] == "dallas"
        assert c.get("/api/hubs/atlantis/breakdown", headers=CODE).status_code == 404
        assert "severity_shares" in c.get("/api/methodology", headers=CODE).json()
        h = c.get("/health").json()
        assert h["status"] == "ok" and h["hubs_scored"] == 47 and "OPENAI" not in str(h)


def test_ui_and_assets_are_served(make_client):
    with make_client() as c:
        page = c.get("/")
        assert page.status_code == 200 and "Weather Risk Agent" in page.text
        for asset in ("/app.js", "/styles.css", "/vendor/marked.min.js", "/vendor/purify.min.js",
                      "/fonts/inter-latin-wght-normal.woff2"):
            assert c.get(asset).status_code == 200, asset


def test_outlook_endpoint(make_client):
    with make_client() as c:
        o = c.get("/api/outlook", params={"month": 9, "top_n": 3}, headers=CODE).json()
        assert o["month_name"] == "September" and len(o["hubs"]) == 3
        assert all(d["title"] for h in o["hubs"] for d in h["past_fema_disasters_this_month"])
        assert c.get("/api/outlook", params={"month": 0}, headers=CODE).status_code == 422


def test_guards_units():
    rl = RateLimiter(2)
    assert [rl.allow("ip", 0), rl.allow("ip", 1), rl.allow("ip", 2), rl.allow("ip", 61)] == [True, True, False, True]
    b = DailyBudget(1.0)
    b.add(0.6)
    assert b.available()
    b.add(0.5)
    assert not b.available() and b.status()["remaining_usd"] == 0

    c.executemany("INSERT INTO hubs (id, name, state, region, lat, lon, county_fips) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'South', ?, ?, '00000')",
                  HUBS)
    c.commit()
    yield c
    c.close()


def fetcher(responses: dict):
    """Fake fetch: responses maps hub latitude to a feature list, or to an exception to raise."""
    def fetch(lat, lon):
        r = responses.get(lat, [])
        if isinstance(r, Exception):
            raise r
        return r
    return fetch


class Recorder:
    """Fake webhook that records what was posted, or fails when asked to."""

    def __init__(self, fail: Exception | None = None):
        self.payloads, self.fail = [], fail

    def __call__(self, url, payload):
        if self.fail:
            raise self.fail
        self.payloads.append(payload)


def check(conn, responses, post=None, url="https://example.test/hook", t="2026-11-23T18:00:00+00:00"):
    return monitor.run_check(conn, fetch=fetcher(responses), post=post or Recorder(), webhook_url=url, checked_at=t)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- parsing


def test_parse_keeps_only_real_active_warnings_of_tracked_types():
    types = monitor.warning_types()
    features = [
        feature(FLOOD_NEW),                                                    # kept
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.FA.A.0002.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", "Flood Watch"),       # watch: ignored
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.CF.Y.0003.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", "Coastal Flood Advisory"),  # advisory
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.FL.W.0004.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", "Flood Warning"),     # river gauge: not tracked
        feature("/T.NEW.KJAX.FA.W.0005.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/"),           # test product class: ignored
        feature("/O.NEW.KJAX.FA.W.0006.261123T1800Z-261124T0000Z/", status="Exercise"),    # exercise: ignored
        feature("/O.CAN.KJAX.FA.W.0008.000000T0000Z-261124T0000Z/"),           # cancelled: no longer active
    ]
    active = monitor.parse_active(features, types)
    assert list(active) == ["KJAX.FA.W.0001"] and active["KJAX.FA.W.0001"].hazard == "flood"


def test_an_extension_keeps_the_same_event_key():
    types = monitor.warning_types()
    assert monitor.parse_active([feature(FLOOD_NEW)], types).keys() == \
        monitor.parse_active([feature(FLOOD_EXT)], types).keys()

def test_first_check_is_a_baseline_not_new_alerts(conn):
    hook = Recorder()
    s = check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, post=hook)
    assert s["baseline"] and s["active_at_start"] == 1 and s["issued"] == 0 and s["active_now"] == 1
    assert "active when monitoring started" in hook.payloads[0]["text"]


def test_new_warning_is_issued_then_ended(conn):
    check(conn, {})                                                     # baseline with nothing active
    hook = Recorder()
    s = check(conn, {29.0: [feature(WINTER_NEW, "Winter Storm Warning")]}, post=hook, t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    assert (s["issued"], s["ended"], s["active_now"], s["webhook"]) == (1, 0, 1, "sent")
    assert "Beta, TX: Winter Storm Warning issued" in hook.payloads[0]["text"]
    s = check(conn, {}, t="2026-11-23T18:30:00+00:00")                 # no longer listed by NWS
    assert (s["issued"], s["ended"], s["active_now"]) == (0, 1, 0)


def test_update_of_the_same_warning_is_not_a_new_alert(conn):
    check(conn, {})
    check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    s = check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_EXT, ends="2026-11-26T07:00:00-05:00")]}, t="2026-11-23T18:30:00+00:00")
    assert (s["issued"], s["ended"], s["active_now"]) == (0, 0, 1)
    assert conn.execute("SELECT ends FROM active_warnings").fetchone()[0] == "2026-11-26T07:00:00-05:00"


def test_failed_request_leaves_the_hub_unchanged(conn):
    check(conn, {})
    check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")
    s = check(conn, {30.0: RuntimeError("NWS API unavailable")}, t="2026-11-23T18:30:00+00:00")
    assert s["hubs_failed"] == ["alpha"] and s["ended"] == 0 and s["active_now"] == 1


def test_webhook_failure_is_recorded_without_the_url(conn):
    class HTTPStatusError(Exception):

    s = check(conn, {30.0: [feature(FLOOD_NEW)]}, post=Recorder(fail=HTTPStatusError("404 for url https://secret.test/x")),
              t="2026-11-23T18:15:00+00:00")

The right half is the running web service, which only reads the database. This split keeps answers fast and reproducible, and the live demo does not depend on any external data API being available. PLAN.md the implementation plan written at the start (kept as part of the AI session record) requirements.txt pinned Python dependencies .env.example configuration template (API key, access code, limits) app/ config.py settings from .env (model, effort, prices for cost tracking, limits) db.py SQLite schema geo.py distance helpers agent.py the agent loop cli.py command-line chat api/ main.py FastAPI app guards.py access code, rate limit, daily budget web/ index.html, styles.css, app.js, plus vendored libraries and font data/ hubs.yaml the hub list (configuration, not code) risk.db the built database (committed so the app runs without downloading anything) evals/ cases.yaml, checks.py, run_evals.py, results/ tests/ unit and integration tests (no OpenAI calls) docs/ai-session/ the exported AI session ``` | GET | `/api/methodology` | Definitions, severity shares, sources and limitations | | POST | `/api/admin/budget` | Raise or lower the daily spend cap while running (admin token) | | GET | `/health` | Database status, data freshness, model, remaining budget | The leaderboard, outlook and hub panel use the same tool functions as the agent, so the numbers on screen and in answers always agree. **Protection for a public URL**: an access code on every `/api/*` call, 10 chat messages per minute per IP address, and a daily OpenAI spend cap (3 USD by default, adjustable at runtime) after which chat answers with a clear message while the data views keep working. **Voice**: voice runs entirely in the browser through the Web Speech API, so the server, the agent and the cost are unchanged. - *Speaking a question*: the microphone button turns speech into text in the input box. The text is not sent automatically: speech recognition sometimes mishears place names, and a wrong hub name would produce a confident answer to the wrong question, so the user checks the text and presses Enter. The button is hidden in browsers without speech recognition (for example Firefox), and errors such as a blocked microphone get a plain message. ## Deploy (Render) The repository includes a `Dockerfile` and a Render Blueprint (`render.yaml`). The image contains the committed database, so the service starts without downloading data. 1. In Render, choose New, then Blueprint, and connect this GitHub repository. Render reads `render.yaml` and creates one Docker web service. 2. Enter the three secrets when asked: `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `APP_ACCESS_CODE` (the code users type in the web app) and `ADMIN_TOKEN` (for changing the daily budget at runtime). The model, reasoning effort, daily budget and rate limit are already set in `render.yaml`. 3. Wait for the build to finish and open the service URL. `/health` should report the database and model. On Render's free plan the service sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic, and the first request after that takes about a minute. Open the URL shortly before a demo. To run the same image locally: ```powershell docker build -t weather-risk-agent . docker run --env-file .env -p 8000:8000 weather-risk-agent ```

The button is hidden in browsers without speech recognition (for example Firefox), and errors such as a blocked microphone get a plain message. ## Deploy (Render) The repository includes a `Dockerfile` and a Render Blueprint (`render.yaml`). The image contains the committed database, so the service starts without downloading data. 1. In Render, choose New, then Blueprint, and connect this GitHub repository. Enter the three secrets when asked: `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `APP_ACCESS_CODE` (the code users type in the web app) and `ADMIN_TOKEN` (for changing the daily budget at runtime). The model, reasoning effort, daily budget and rate limit are already set in `render.yaml`. 3. Wait for the build to finish and open the service URL. `/health` should report the database and model. We chose three simple ones: an access code, a per-IP rate limit, and a daily spend cap (3 USD by default) that an admin can change while the service runs. The leaderboard and hub details keep working after the cap is reached because they do not use the model.
-## D13. What we chose not to build
+## D13. Alerts: live warnings instead of score changes
+**The assignment's bonus:** a scheduled or webhook alert when a hub's risk score changes.
+- A. Literal score-change alerts: refresh the data on a schedule, re-score, alert when a score or tier changes.
+- B. Live warning alerts: alert when an NWS warning starts or ends at a hub.
+- C. Not building alerts, and describing the design instead.

+**Why.** Our scores are 20-year averages; one more day of data almost never moves them, so option A would rarely fire and would mostly demonstrate plumbing. What changes day to day is whether a hub is under an active warning, which is the operational question ("which hubs are disrupted right now?") next to the historical one the scores answer. It also reuses the same warning types and the same "warning area must contain the hub" idea as the scoring, so the live and historical views agree on what counts. C was considered because of the submission deadline; B was built as an isolated module with its own tables and tests, so it cannot affect the scores or the chat.

+- *Scheduler outside the server (GitHub Actions, every 15 minutes).* An in-process timer would stop whenever the free-plan server sleeps; an external call wakes it. The job does nothing until the repository has the app URL and admin token configured.
+- *Warnings identified by VTEC event id.* NWS reissues a warning many times (updates, extensions); using the message id would report each update as a new alert.
+- *Failed requests change nothing.* Otherwise an API outage would look like every warning ending at once, followed by a burst of "new" warnings.
+- *Baseline on a fresh database.* After a redeploy the alert state is empty; announcing every active warning as new would be wrong, so they are reported as active when monitoring started.
+- *No webhook URL in errors or logs.* The scheduler's logs are public for a public repository, and a Slack webhook URL works like a password.
+## D14. What we chose not to build
- **MCP server:** useful but not required; the tool registry would make it a thin wrapper.

+- **Live warnings in the chat and leaderboard:** the monitor's data could become an agent tool and a hub badge; left out to keep the agent focused on historical risk.

**Protection for a public URL**: an access code on every `/api/*` call, 10 chat messages per minute per IP address, and a daily OpenAI spend cap (3 USD by default, adjustable at runtime) after which chat answers with a clear message while the data views keep working.

+**Live warning alerts** (the assignment's bonus, `app/alerts/monitor.py`). The risk scores describe 20 years of history and change only when the data is rebuilt, so an alert on "score changed" would almost never fire. What does change day to day is whether a hub is under an active warning right now, so the monitor alerts on that:
+- Every 15 minutes a GitHub Actions job calls `POST /api/admin/alerts/check`. The schedule lives outside the server because the free plan puts the server to sleep; the call wakes it.

+- The check asks the NWS alerts API which alerts are active at each hub's point (47 requests in parallel, about 18 seconds) and keeps only real warnings (status Actual, significance W) of the types the scoring uses. Watches, advisories and test messages are ignored.

+- Each warning is identified by its VTEC event id (office, type and event number), which stays the same through updates and extensions. Comparing with the previous check gives the warnings that were issued or ended; each becomes a row in `hub_alerts` and all of them go out in one webhook message (Slack format), for example "Oakland, CA: Coastal Flood Warning issued, until 2026-11-26 16:00 local time".

+- Safeguards: a failed request leaves that hub unchanged (an API error never reads as "warning ended"); the first check on a fresh database is a baseline that reports warnings as "active when monitoring started" instead of new; only one check runs at a time; delivery errors are recorded with the error type only, never the webhook URL, because the scheduler logs of a public repository are public.

+- Limitations: alert history is stored in SQLite on the server's temporary disk and is lost on redeploy (a production version would use a persistent database); GitHub may start scheduled runs a few minutes late.

The text is not sent automatically: speech recognition sometimes mishears place names, and a wrong hub name would produce a confident answer to the wrong question, so the user checks the text and presses Enter. The button is hidden in browsers without speech recognition (for example Firefox), and errors such as a blocked microphone get a plain message.

content.text:
Green means the job ran, but it also shows green when it skips because a setting is missing. First, confirm it really ran a check: click **check**, then expand **Run one alert check**. You should see a JSON line containing `"hubs_checked": 47`. If it says "APP_URL or ADMIN_TOKEN is not configured; skipping", one of the two settings is missing or misnamed.

**To see an alert arrive (about 3 minutes):**

1. **Get a test inbox.** Open https://webhook.site. It creates a unique URL for you right away (`https://webhook.site/...`). Copy it and keep the tab open.
2. **Give it to the app.** In Render, open your service, go to **Environment**, add `ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` = that URL, and click **Save**. Render restarts the service, which takes about a minute.
3. **Run the workflow again** (Actions, Hub alert check, Run workflow).

The restart clears the alert state, so this run is a fresh baseline. If any hub currently has an active warning (Oakland had a Coastal Flood Warning an hour ago), a message appears within seconds in the webhook.site tab, like:

```
Hub weather alerts (check at 2026-11-23 19:40 UTC)
- Oakland, CA: Coastal Flood Warning active when monitoring started, until 2026-11-26 16:00 local time
```

From then on, every 15 minutes a message arrives only when a warning starts ("issued") or ends ("ended") at a hub. If no hub has an active warning at that moment, the baseline sends nothing, and the first message comes when weather changes.

**To see the recorded alerts without a webhook:** open https://weather-risk-agent-gz90.onrender.com/docs. Find **GET /api/alerts**, click **Try it out**, enter your access code in the `x-access-code` field, and click **Execute**. It lists the warnings active now, recent alerts and the result of the last check.

The messages contain only hub names and public NWS warning text, so a public test service like webhook.site is fine for this. For a real setup you'd use a Slack incoming webhook instead.

content.text:
**Is there a real risk? Low, but not zero.** Here's what someone with the access code could and couldn't do:

- **They could:** use the app like a reviewer, which means chatting and viewing data. Each chat costs money, but the $3 daily cap and the 10-messages-per-minute limit bound it. The realistic worst case is someone using up the day's budget, so chat shows "budget used" for the rest of that day while the leaderboard and data views keep working. If that happened on interview day, you'd raise the cap with your admin token in one command.
- **They couldn't:** see or use your OpenAI key, change the budget or any setting (that needs the admin token, which is separate and was never shown), or modify any data.
- **Where it could leak from:** the transcript gets committed to your **public** GitHub repo, so anyone browsing it could see the screenshot. That's why removing it from the export matters, and with that done, keeping the same code is fine.
